title: GOP shifts midterm priorities as concerns turn to defending seats in red states
description: Republicans are playing defense deep in their own territory as voter anger over price hikes puts more House and Senate seats in play in the midterms.
fullText:
Republicans are playing defense deep in their own territory as voter anger over price hikes puts more House and Senate seats in play in the midterms.

New rounds of big spending, visits from Trump administration officials and private conversations among top GOP officials overseeing the battle for control of Congress reveal a party rushing to shore up red seats and states President Donald Trump won handily in 2024.

In the House, the fight has expanded far outside the few-dozen seats considered the most competitive as Republicans start to unleash their massive warchest: Since Aug. 1, more than $110 million in ad bookings have gone toward Republican-held districts so red that Trump won them by double digits.

In the Senate, Republicans are racing to shore up Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted as the Midwest struggles under the weight of Trump's tariffs and high diesel prices. Trump and Vice President JD Vance are both expected to travel to the state before the midterms to boost Husted, according to four people familiar with the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss not-yet-public plans.

GOP leaders are also trying to keep a handle on contests in Iowa and Kansas — and they've quietly begun deprioritizing Georgia and even North Carolina, which a growing number of Republicans are privately bracing for Democrats to flip.

"We need to stop the contagion," said one senior GOP official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the midterm landscape.

"The map is hilariously big right now," said one national Republican pollster.

Since Aug. 1, nearly two-thirds of advertising funds in House races have been booked or spent in races with GOP incumbents, according to a POLITICO analysis of data from AdImpact, which tracks political advertising.

That includes nearly $18 million to embattled Rep. Max Miller in Ohio's 7th District; $14.6 million to Texas' 15th District where Monica De La Cruz faces a challenge from Tejano Singer Bobby Pulido; $9.6 million in Alaska where Rep. Nick Begich faces a challenge from independent Bill Hill; and millions more to other districts that Trump carried by double digits two years ago.

The GOP holds a massive cash advantage over Democrats — which, for now, means they can afford to spend more broadly. Republican groups are dividing up the spending deluge in the final weeks ahead of the midterms, with Trump's MAGA Inc. affiliated super PAC spending heavily to shore up safer red seats and deter Democrats from pushing into those races.

"The voter enthusiasm [for Republican voters] is not where it needs to be but that's where a money advantage can make a really big impact," said Mark Bednar, a GOP strategist and former communications director for then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy.

Republicans have adjusted their Senate map expectations: They're still bullish about Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. They're not as optimistic about North Carolina — which Trump won in 2024 — but they are hoping to force Democrats to spend more there.

Republicans are more concerned about Alaska and Texas. And their worries about Ohio have escalated amid soaring diesel prices and backlash to tariffs — challenges they're also confronting in Texas, Iowa, Michigan and Kansas.

Already two battleground candidates have called for ends to the Iran war, pointing to the high prices: Iowa GOP Senate nominee Ashley Hinson, whose team has grown increasingly wary of the tight race and Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers. Both Hinson and Rogers use top Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio to guide their campaigns.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment on Hinson's and Rogers' remarks.

Senior GOP operatives' own internal polling shows Trump's approval underwater in deep red states across the country. And an Iowa poll conducted last week by a Democratic-leaning pollster found Democrat Josh Turek with a one-point lead in the Senate race and Trump's approval at 43 percent in the state he won by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, according to a copy of the poll obtained by POLITICO.

"As more races come online, it very clearly is a defensive map for Republicans across the country," said a national GOP strategist working on multiple battleground races.

In Ohio, Republicans are optimistic that their attacks on former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown's voting record are starting to break through, based on recent internal polling. But they've been conveying to outside groups for weeks that they need help reinforcing vulnerable incumbents like Husted. On Monday, the pro-crypto super PAC Fairshake said it planned to unleash $30 million against Brown, who was the top Democrat on the Banking Committee before losing reelection in 2024 — fueled in part by more than $40 million against him from Fairshake that year.

"The stakes go far beyond one Senate seat," Amy Natoce, a Husted campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. "Control of the Senate will determine which agenda moves forward in Washington: Sherrod Brown's out-of-touch socialist agenda, or Jon Husted's agenda of lower taxes, a secure border, and an economy that rewards hard work."

One Michigan Republican acknowledged the immense weight of the tariffs in races across the battleground state — including in the marquee Senate contest between Rogers and progressive Abdul El-Sayed, as well as across competitive House races.

"Everywhere we go, we are getting hammered on it," the Michigan Republican said. "It's crushing us."

Even skeptical Republicans have been quietly checking in with their colleagues to see if the panic in redder territory is borne out in reality on the ground or just overblown polling. One GOP lawmaker who spoke to Hinson and her campaign team was somewhat surprised by their answers.

"It's real," that House Republican told POLITICO.

And POLITICO overheard a senior member of Kansas' Republican party leadership complaining about their state's tighter-than-expected race at the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month. GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, the person said, was in some trouble even as Republicans tried to dismiss the seriousness of his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton.

Trump and Vance, meanwhile, continue to travel to states they won by double digits in 2024 to stump for Republican candidates, as Trump-aligned super PACs hammer the airwaves in far more red territory than blue.

Recently-formed super PACs aligned with MAGA Inc. — Trump's main spending vehicle that holds more than $400 million — have spent in 42 House districts so far, 30 defensive and 12 offensive. On average, they are spending in areas that voted for Trump by 7.9 points in 2024, according to a POLITICO analysis.

The PACs are even spending in some districts Trump carried by 15 points as a way to shore up Republicans and deter Democratic advances, according to Republicans involved in the conversations.

Major Republican super PACs, including the Trump aligned-super PACs and party-linked groups, have spent in more than two dozen GOP-held seats where Trump won by at least 5 points in 2024.

"Republicans aren't taking anything for granted this cycle and will deploy whatever resources necessary to protect our majorities and prevent Democrats from taking control," RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement.

The NRSC argued that "Democrats lack quality candidates and a clear path to victory," so the party is "feigning optimism" and looking to candidates who have lost before, including Brown, "to somehow deliver [a] majority." The NRCC said their opposition is "too broke to fight back."

The geography of the Senate map still favors the GOP this cycle: Democrats have to defend all of their seats, while flipping four Republican-held ones, to take control of the upper chamber.

Republicans believe they have a real shot at flipping New Hampshire, and public polling shows Minnesota's Senate race closer than expected, forcing Democrats to pay some minor attention to a state Kamala Harris won in 2024.

And Republicans are still hopeful that their mid-decade gerrymandering push could still give them a structural advantage as they fight to defend the House. Republicans won the redistricting war that erupted last summer and will likely net at least six seats from it.

But as economic concerns continue to dominate — with little relief in sight — Democrats are growing increasingly bullish.

"You know, I look at places like Kansas where I never thought we'd have a chance, or South Carolina or even Mississippi, these places are longshots, but they look like they're competitive," Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) said.

For their part, senior Republicans have been working the problem from two ends, trying to gently persuade Trump in private conversations to back off some of his recent policy moves and wind down the war in Iran — while also organizing a wave of cash reinforcements across the growing map to try to stem the bleeding.

GOP lawmakers pressed Trump officials at their Dallas convention and since then to take emergency actions around fuel prices and refinery capacity. A band of House Republicans led an unsuccessful attempt to vote on a federal gas tax suspension until after Election Day. And, over the weekend, Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) posted several direct appeals to Trump, asking why he hasn't put an embargo on diesel exports.

But many are convinced the bleeding won't stop until voters get some relief at the pump.

"The question is: How much longer can we go?" one senior House Republican said.

title: Tony White takes responsibility for FSU defense
description: Defensive coordinator Tony White says he is to blame for Florida State's defensive struggles against Alabama.
fullText:
Florida State's defense has faced mounting scrutiny through the first three games of the season, and defensive coordinator Tony White made it clear Monday that he believes much of the responsibility falls on him.

The Seminoles surrendered 567 yards in Saturday's loss to Alabama, allowing the Crimson Tide to score on nine consecutive possessions after a promising start defensively. Florida State opened the game by forcing five straight third-down stops, but once Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell found his rhythm in the second half, the Seminoles had no answers.

White said the collapse reminded him of last season's loss to Virginia, when Florida State was unable to make a critical stop late in the game, eventually forcing overtime and suffering its first defeat of the season.

"It starts with me first," White said.

"I mean, that's my fault. I should've stayed aggressive, should've stayed attacking. Sometimes when you get hit on a play or something, you kind of look at the call and say, 'OK, that didn't work, so let me not call that.' We were calling that all in the first half. They made a play. Guess what? Call it again on the next play. And we hit it again for one or two yards. So I just got to be really critical of myself and make sure that the guys who were doing well keep having confidence in that and let them go play."

More: Mike Norvell: FSU RB Samuel Singleton Jr. FSU RB out for extended time

White repeatedly pointed to his own play-calling decisions while reflecting on what went wrong against Alabama. After coming close to upsetting the eighth-ranked Crimson Tide for a second consecutive season, Florida State could not maintain its early defensive momentum.

The defensive struggles have been evident throughout the opening three games. The Seminoles enter this week with a 1-2 record and have allowed 1,471 total yards and 94 points.

Florida State generated four turnovers in its loss to SMU, but the defense failed to force a takeaway against Alabama. The Seminoles also rank 117th nationally in pressure rate, a concerning statistic for a unit built around White's aggressive philosophy.

"It was me," White said. "I'm always going to stand up in here and tell you the truth. It was me. I shouldn't have stayed aggressive, stayed attacking. The guys were on fire. They were humming, chasing ghosts up there.

"There were some defenses that were really good, and we gave up a big play, and I didn't even call it again because I didn't even see the defensive efficiency deal on there. So I should have called it about 10 more times. I need to be better at that and let those guys play."

More: Final: Alabama extends Seminoles' woes, FSU tumbles 50-36

Despite the disappointing performance, White praised his defense's effort in one of college football's toughest environments at Bryant-Denny Stadium.

He highlighted several young contributors, including defensive linemen Kevin "JuJu" Wynn and Darryll Desir, for making positive impressions against Alabama.

While White openly accepted responsibility for the breakdowns against the Crimson Tide, he said the focus now shifts to correcting mistakes and restoring confidence within the unit. The team, which also took accountability as White fully disclosed in their team meeting, is still all in.

Florida State will have an opportunity to do just that Saturday when it hosts Central Arkansas at 3 p.m. at Doak Campbell Stadium. For White and the Seminoles, the challenge is straightforward: learn from a costly collapse and rediscover the aggressive identity that helped make the defense successful in the first place.

"In terms of confidence, no, it's had nothing to do with confidence. It's all about the process, White said.

"As you look at what works, what doesn't, and really it's the players. You look at them and how they believe, right? You don't play that hard and not believe in what you're doing and not having an answer for things, you know? Like you don't play that hard and not trust the coaches, not trust the staff, not trust the process that we have. So they believe, they see it."

White's accountability may not erase the frustration of Florida State's defensive collapse against Alabama, but it offers a clear starting point as the Seminoles look to reverse their early-season struggles. With conference play looming and a defense searching for consistency, Florida State has little time to dwell on missed opportunities. The response against Central Arkansas could provide an early indication of whether White's self-assessment leads to the defensive turnaround the Seminoles desperately need.

title: Ja’Marr Chase says defense is the Bengals’ ‘backbone’ this season
description: The revamped defense continues impressive start.
fullText:
The Cincinnati Bengals made it clear this offseason that they were all in on revamping a roster that missed the postseason three years in a row.

The Bengals brought in so many decorated veterans like Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, and Bryan Cook to create a new culture and create it as quickly as possible.

Through the first two weeks of play, that investment is showing, and it's showing as quickly as the front office had hoped.

The Bengals defense dominated both the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Houston Texans, which has stunned the NFL world.

After a two-touchdown day this past weekend, Ja'Marr Chase shared his thoughts on the defense so far and gave that unit some major props.

"I can't even describe how much I love our defense right now," Chase stated. "They're our backbone. We're going to feed off their energy."

Chase has never shied away from speaking his truth to the media, and he showed love for a unit that has not complemented the Bengals offense the past few years.

The Bengals are officially 2-0 to start a season in the Burrow-Taylor era with Joe Burrow healthy going into week 3.

title: Vermont man convicted of attempted murder in shooting of 3 Palestinian college students
description:
Burlington, Vt. (AP) — A jury on Monday convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defense rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies.
Jason Eaton faces up to life in prison in the November 2023 attack in Burlington, which paralyzed Hisham Awartani from the waist down and wounded his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid.
fullText:
Burlington, Vt. (AP) — A jury on Monday convicted a Vermont man of attempted murder in the shootings of three Palestinian college students who were walking near his home, rejecting an insanity defense rooted in his claims that he was acting on orders from U.S. and Israeli intelligence agencies.

Jason Eaton faces up to life in prison in the November 2023 attack in Burlington, which paralyzed Hisham Awartani from the waist down and wounded his friends, Tahseen Aliahmad and Kinnan Abdalhamid.

The men, all 20 at the time, had been visiting Awartani's grandmother for Thanksgiving. They were smoking cigarettes and speaking a mix of English and Arabic as they walked near the University of Vermont campus after dusk. Two of them were wearing traditional Palestinian scarves known as keffiyehs.

The jury deliberated for several hours before reaching its verdict after a weeklong trial that saw testimony from the three men, who recounted how their stroll ended in bloodshed, and defense and prosecution psychiatric experts who offered differing views of Eaton's mental health and criminal culpability.

Eaton, 51, stared ahead blankly as the verdict was read, standing alongside his lawyers — public defenders whom he tried to fire last week over his concerns that his defense hadn't been "adequately presented." Judge John Pacht, who blocked Eaton's midtrial bid to act as his own lawyer, ordered him jailed pending sentencing, which has yet to be scheduled.

Awartani and Aliahmad watched from the front row of the courtroom gallery, smiling and hugging people around them.

"The verdict cannot undo what happened or erase the trauma our families still carry, but it affirms something fundamental: Jason Eaton is responsible for what he did," Awartani's mother, Elizabeth Price, told reporters afterward.

Eaton had pleaded not guilty but did not dispute that he was the shooter. He claimed that the CIA and Mossad transmitted their orders via FM radio and that God was commanding him to protect his Jewish neighbors. His lawyers had urged jurors to find him not guilty by reason of insanity, an outcome that would've spared him from prison but could have required that he undergo mental health treatment.

Eaton's lawyers, Margaret Jansch and Joshua O'Hara, said he had struggled with mental health issues his whole life, including diagnoses of attention deficit, post-traumatic stress, bipolar, depression and borderline personality disorders, culminating in a psychotic break after losing his job at a credit union two weeks before the shooting.

Prosecutor Sarah George countered that Eaton was a narcissist but not legally insane. He had a grandiose sense of self-importance and lacked empathy but was fully aware of the criminality of his conduct, George said in a closing argument. He appeared nervous when police arrived at his door, repeatedly asked for a lawyer and hasn't claimed to have received any other messages directing his actions, she said.

Eaton told officers that he had a shotgun in his apartment, but didn't disclose that he had other weapons, including a Ruger .380-caliber handgun that was found in a bedroom dresser and that crime lab testing concluded was used in the shooting, said George, the Chittenden County state's attorney.

The shooting, weeks after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, shook Burlington, and reverberated in the West Bank, where the three wounded men grew up and became friends as schoolmates in Ramallah before moving to the U.S. for college. It spawned calls for a hate crime investigation.

But no hate crime charges were filed as questions persisted about whether anti-Palestinian animus, an altered mental state or something else had compelled Eaton to open fire. After the verdict, Awartani's mother said Eaton's hateful rhetoric, aired at the trial, had made it clear why he targeted her son.

Days after the shooting, George said in her closing argument, Eaton had told his lawyers that he wished Awartani's grandmother had warned him that the men were "going to dress up like terrorists" and trek through his neighborhood.

"Or see, if grandma had said to them, you know, maybe now's not a great time to wear that thing on your head," George said, paraphrasing Eaton's remarks. "You know, things are a little tense when you've got American hostages over in Palestine, and we're trying to get them back."

"They were not the words of a man confused about who he shot or why," Elizabeth Price said. "They were the words a man who saw three young men speaking the language of their childhood and wearing what made them feel closer to their far away families and homes and decided to kill them because of his own prejudices."

Awartani testified last week that he first noticed Eaton standing on a porch as they approached the apartment house where he lived. Within seconds, Awartani said, Eaton was off the porch and walking toward them. His face was expressionless and he didn't say anything. As Eaton got to about 5 to 10 feet (1.5 to 3 meters) away, "he pulled out a handgun and started shooting at us," Awartani said.

Abdalhamid, a student at Haverford College near Philadelphia, said he fled and hid behind another home after seeing Aliahmad fall to the ground. He said he only realized later when he sat down that he had also been wounded.

Awartani, who was studying at Brown University in Rhode Island at the time, was shot in the chest and the bullet ricocheted off his scapula, causing paraplegia in his spinal cord. Aliahmad, who was a student at Trinity College in Connecticut, was struck in the collarbone, and Abdalhamid was shot in the right buttock.

Jacob Pyne, who lived in a different apartment in the same house as Eaton, testified that he heard four to six gunshots, followed by footsteps going up the stairs of the apartment house. He said he ran outside and heard two men speaking, one of whom was more vocal and yelling, "I've been shot, help me." He then brought the men blankets and called 911.

Eaton didn't testify. In an opening statement last week, O'Hara told jurors that Eaton claimed he started receiving messages while listening to a local NPR affiliate. At first, the messages were encouraging and validating, the lawyer said, but subsequent messages turned dark, insisting that Eaton "has to go out and shoot somebody."

title: Defense clamps down after Week 1 tackling woes, fueling Broncos' 20-13 comeback win over Jaguars
description: The Denver Broncos ' defense went back to the basics after a disastrous opener in Kansas City.  The defense limited Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville offense to three points in the second half — and none over the final 24 minutes — allowing Bo Nix to stage a comeback as the Broncos rallied for a 20-13 win Sunday.  “Look, our job is to play the game and give the ball to the offense,” linebacker Alex Singleton said after his defense's rebound.
fullText:
DENVER (AP) — The Denver Broncos ' defense went back to the basics after a disastrous opener in Kansas City. It focused on the most fundamental part of football there is — tackling.

The defense limited Trevor Lawrence and the Jacksonville offense to three points in the second half — and none over the final 24 minutes — allowing Bo Nix to stage a comeback as the Broncos rallied for a 20-13 win Sunday.

"Look, our job is to play the game and give the ball to the offense," linebacker Alex Singleton said after his defense's rebound.

A job made easier by simply wrapping up.

The Broncos re-emphasized fundamentals all week after missing a whopping 28 tackles in a 31-10 loss to Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs. They held the Jaguars under 100 yards rushing Sunday and kept Lawrence out of the end zone after he threw for three TDs and ran for another in a 34-20 win in Denver last December.

"It was being better this week and being one step better, having that short-term memory," Pat Surtain II explained. "Erase that week and just focus on this week ahead."

The Broncos (1-1) were one of the top defenses in the league last season, but it wasn't on display in Week 1. That could possibly be chalked up to not playing all that many snaps in the preseason.

One thing's for sure — the team's confidence never wavered.

"It's funny how everyone was freaking out after one game," defensive lineman Zach Allen said. "We got back on track today."

Trailing 13-3 in the third quarter, the defense dug in as Nix and the offense found their groove in reeling off 17 straight points to snap the Jaguars' nine-game regular-season winning streak.

The Jaguars finished the game by going interception, missed field goal and punt. The Broncos' last four drives looked like this: field goal, TD, TD and victory formation.

"It was a good day for the team to bounce back," said cornerback Riley Moss, who picked off Lawrence's pass late in the third quarter. "There's still things that we've got to work on. It wasn't a perfect game, but we got the 'W.'"

Last December, Lawrence threw for 279 yards and three TDs with no interceptions. This time, it was a different story. Lawrence threw for 138 yards in the first half but only 51 more the rest of the way. What's more, the Broncos held the Jaguars to 2 of 6 on third-down conversions in the second half.

"As as far what they did, it wasn't anything that surprised us," Lawrence said. "They played really good up front. They got after us a little bit and I thought we played on our heels a little bit."

In constant pursuit was pass rusher Nik Bonitto, who had three QB hits. He led a group that kept constant pressure on Lawrence.

"They're a great offense," Bonitto said. "But at the same time, we look at last year's game and we see it was really just missed tackles that gave them a lot of points and even this year making sure that we're playing to our standard."

One of the biggest sequences of the game was in the third quarter and the Jaguars facing a first-and-goal at the 9. Denver held them to a field goal to make it 13-3 and keep the game in range.

"We made game-changing plays," said Surtain, whose team hosts the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday night. "That's what we did — just finding ways to get them off the field, finding ways to win third down. That was huge."

AP freelancer Ashlyn Stapleton contributed to this report.

title: Three Keys For the Miami Heat to Win the Eastern Conference
description: Building around a newly acquired Giannis Antetokounmpo, the Miami Heat must leverage elite interior defense and veteran perimeter shooting to overcome injury concerns and reclaim Eastern Conference dominance this upcoming season.
fullText:
MIAMI, Fla. – As training camp is on the horizon, here are three keys for the Miami Heat to win the Eastern Conference Finals in the 2026-27 NBA season:

Like the popular saying goes, "the best ability is availability." This take primarily falls upon Giannis Antetokounmpo, who played just 36 games last season; a new career low by a significant margin. The 10-time All-Star battled a calf injury and then the Milwaukee Bucks load-managed him. Antetokounmpo, when available last season, averaged 27.6 points on 62.4 percent shooting, 9.8 rebounds, and 5.4 assists.

Also, Klay Thompson and Tim Hardaway Jr., two of the Heat's free-agent signings, are over the age of 33. Both sharpshooters will get meaningful playing time, but putting a heavy workload on their shoulders should be taken with precaution.

Given the personnel, the Heat should have one of the best defenses in the league. Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo each received at least five All-Defensive selections. The Heat's new frontcourt duo should be difficult to score over, especially in the paint.

Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins are two underrated defenders who don't get enough credit. They can both guard the perimeter and inside the arc. Despite being undersized (listed at 6'0), Mitchell shouldn't be classified as a lesser matchup. Wiggins, like Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, can guard multiple positions.

Coming off the bench are Bobby Portis Jr. and Pelle Larsson, both of whom are scrappy defenders.

As the saying goes, "defense wins championships." The Heat have the right personnel to live up to the phrase.

After acquiring Antetokounmpo in a blockbuster trade, the Heat needed to surround him with the right pieces, especially outside shooting. As the 31-year-old looks to dominate the paint, he will draw more attention to the defense, creating open looks for others.

Thompson and Hardaway Jr. were critical signees to provide Antetokounmpo floor spacing. Plus, the Heat retained three players (Wiggins, Mitchell, and Simone Fontecchio) who shot over 35 percent from behind the arc last season.

Following an eventful offseason, this team has the components to compete for a championship and win the Eastern Conference Finals. The Heat are among the early favorites, along with the Philadelphia 76ers, New York Knicks, and Boston Celtics. It's been 13 years since the last Larry O'Brien trophy made South Florida its home and a parade went down Biscayne Blvd. The current Heat team is looking to change that.

fullText:
Liverpool travel to Bournemouth for a 2 pm BST Premier League clash at Vitality Stadium. As of Sunday morning, both clubs have reported no fresh injury concerns following their midweek matches.

The official starting lineups are expected about an hour before kickoff, so the main selection questions remain around Liverpool's midfield and defense and Bournemouth's rotation after their European trip.

Liverpool remain without four players, while Bournemouth have four confirmed absentees. Andoni Iraola also returns to Bournemouth for the first time since leaving the club in the summer.

The Bournemouth vs Liverpool confirmed team news will settle the remaining questions before the match, with both sides looking to add an important result to their Premier League campaigns.

Liverpool's injury list remains unchanged from Friday. Conor Bradley is unavailable with a knee injury, while Giovanni Leoni is also out with a knee problem. Hugo Ekitike remains sidelined with an Achilles injury, and Federico Chiesa is unavailable because of a back issue.

Joe Gomez returned from a lay-off in Tuesday's 3-1 Carabao Cup win over Tottenham. His next appearance will be his 300th for Liverpool, but he is expected to start on the bench.

Virgil van Dijk is expected to return to the starting lineup alongside Jeremy Jacquet. Ronald Araujo could move to right-back, while Alisson Becker is expected to replace Giorgi Mamardashvili in goal.

Liverpool's expected formation is 4-2-3-1, with Alexander Isak leading the attack. Florian Wirtz should play behind him, with Cody Gakpo and Bradley Barcola on the wings. Alexis Mac Allister and Dominik Szoboszlai are the expected midfield pairing.

Bournemouth also have four players unavailable. Eli Junior Kroupi remains out with a foot injury, while Amine Adli has a calf problem. Veljko Milosavljevic is sidelined with a knee injury and Julian Araujo remains out with a thigh issue.

Marco Rose reported no new injury concerns after Thursday's 2-1 Europa League win at Real Sociedad. He will assess his players after the trip before confirming his Premier League lineup.

Djordje Petrovic is expected to start in goal, with Adam Smith, James Hill, Antonio Silva and Adrien Truffert forming the back four.

Alex Scott is expected to start in midfield. Tyler Adams, Lewis Cook and Ryan Christie are options to partner him.

Rayan, Justin Kluivert and Marcus Tavernier are expected to play behind Francisco Evanilson. Tavernier has been Bournemouth's most productive attacker so far this season.

Bournemouth are still looking for their first Premier League win under Rose. They have drawn with Everton, Newcastle United and Brentford after losing their opening league game. Their European victory at Real Sociedad was the first win in the club's history in that competition.

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Defense keeps searching for takeaways
description: Notes and thoughts on the Patriots defense, the home opener blues, Mike Smith’s connection with Aaron Rodgers, and more.
fullText:
Coming into Week 2 with a loss under their belt, the New England Patriots will try to get their season back on track in front of their home crowd. To do so, they will have to get their revenge against a Pittsburgh Steelers team that managed to beat them the last time they met in 2025.

Naturally, most of our attention this week was on that particular game. However, there is a lot going on at One Patriot Place these days, so let's clean out the notebook.

Welcome to the latest edition of our Sunday Patriots Notes.

The Patriots defense is one of the best in the NFL, but it is lacking in one critical area: taking the ball away. Last regular season, the unit ranked just 19th in the league with 19 takeaways. This year, it failed to record a fumble recovery or interception — while throwing three picks themselves — in the season-opening loss to the Seahawks.

Naturally, the Patriots are looking for ways to get better at creating turnovers.

"We focus on it like crazy," said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr. "We focus on it in training camp, in OTAs, now. It's about the opportunity. Capitalizing on opportunity, in my opinion, is the biggest thing on takeaways. And the way you do that is you get more attempts."

For free agency pickup Kevin Byard, who led the NFL with seven interceptions last season, those attempts need to come within the framework of the defensive structure.

"You can't chase plays," Byard said. "You can't try to go out here and just say we're going to get turnovers and just try to magically just go make a play that's not for you. We have to stay true to the defense, stay true within the scheme. But for us, it's going to be more about trying to get those attempts at the ball.

"When I say attempts at the ball, just like, last week I think Jaylen Warren fumbled the ball, guys swarming the little check-down and the defensive line comes from the line of scrimmage and punches the ball out. I think those are the things that we can probably take to the next step as a defense. I think interceptions will come. Those things come in bunches. Those aren't situations where, if you're playing man coverage, you just turn around and look at the ball and you're not covering your man. I think it's one of those situations where the interceptions will come, but it's more about getting those attempts at the ball carrier."

Of those 19 regular season turnovers mentioned above, nine came in the form of fumble recoveries. That was good enough for 10th in the league. The interceptions, meanwhile, were not on the same level: despite fielding one of the NFL's top cornerbacks in Christian Gonzalez, New England's 10 picks ranked them only 18th.

Gonzalez did come close to an INT last week versus Seattle, but he dropped a Drew Lock pass attempt that landed in his hands. Needless to say, the Pro Bowler wants to get better at finishing plays.

He also thinks the Patriots as a whole need to get better at communicating on the defensive side of the ball.

"It just comes down to communication," he said, "getting us in the right spot and then capitalizing and making the play.

Historically, the Patriots are a pretty good team playing at home. However, Gillette Stadium has witnessed a disappointing streak as of late: between 2021 and 2025, the team has not won a single of its home openers:

2021: 17-16 loss vs. Miami Dolphins

2022: 37-26 loss vs. Baltimore Ravens

2023: 25-20 loss vs. Philadelphia Eagles

2024: 23-20 (OT) loss vs. Seattle Seahawks

2025: 20-13 loss vs. Las Vegas Raiders

The Patriots' last victory in their first home regular season game came in 2020, when quarterback Cam Newton led the team to a 21-11 win over the Miami Dolphins.

The Patriots' defensive quest for takeaways will be without Carlton Davis on Sunday versus Pittsburgh. The starting cornerback was ruled out for the game because of a neck injury, meaning New England will have to adjust at the position.

How? By primarily relying on two players, Marcus Jones and Charles Woods.

"It will be Marcus and Charles Woods that will come in and play a little bit 

Two members of the NFL's 2005 draft class will be in the spotlight on Sunday, albeit in different capacities. On one side, Aaron Rodgers will lead the Steelers offense as its starting quarterback; on the other, Mike Smith will try to help disrupt the future Hall of Famer.

The difference is, Smith will do so not from the field but the sidelines: he is in his second season coaching the Patriots' outside linebackers, despite getting drafted the same year as Rogers.

"It blows my mind," Smith said about their connection. "Somebody said the other day about 2010, I was with the Jets and we played New England in the playoffs. I was like, 'God, that was like 16 years ago.' And I was like, 'Oh my god, wait a minute, 16 years? Aaron Rogers is still playing.' It's like, 'What the heck?' That's just credit to him."

Whereas Rodgers was selected 24th overall in the first round in 2005, Smith remained on the board until the 234th pick in Round 7. His career also was significantly shorter, ending after just four seasons and 14 games. For comparison, Rodgers will start his 280th career game on Sunday.

"One guy had a better career than the other guy," said Mike Vrabel. "He's done it for a lot of years at a very high level, a Hall of Fame player. I guess it's funny to think that they're the same age and they got drafted the same year."

Due to injury and a drawn-out contract negotiation process, second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas had a slow start to his Patriots career and some rough stretches both in training camp and preseason. The season opener against Seattle was a different story, though: while only playing 19 snaps, Jacas registered a sack and a tackle for loss.

"I saw growth and that's what's most important, there is improvement," said Zak Kuhr. "There's going to be bumps and bruises along the way, and he's going to get some good experience. We just have to look through the bumps and bruises and make sure that's not the same mistakes. But I thought he played hard, he played physical, he played fast. Just have to clean up some details and technique. We want this week to look better than last week."

"Just playing a little bit faster, seeing things," added Mike Smith. "It takes time. We still have a long way to go, but things are starting to slow down, starting to recognize for him. We had loads of extra time to prepare for Seattle, but [this] is the player we expected to see and we've just got to continue from where that was at and keep building."

In its first training camp with Zak Kuhr as coordinator, the Patriots defense opted to incorporate more big nickel looks with three safeties on the field. In the season opener versus Seattle, the team used that package on 40% of snaps.

"It gives you some versatility in some calls and some structures," Kuhr explained. "When you play these teams that like to move around a ton, sometimes it just helps you to have that extra second-level defender rather than having a defender on the line of scrimmage. It just gives you some more multiplicity and you can kind of get to some different coverages easier with those guys than with the bigger guys."

When describing the Steelers' identity this week, Mike Vrabel specifically mentioned size and length. It's something no player will be more directly confronted with than Drake Maye.

The Patriots' starting quarterback will not just try to avoid the long reach of edge rushers such as T.J. Watt but also attempt to throw passes through what will be a forest of arms.

"I think it's hard to look at when they're jumping and when they're trying to get hands up," Maye said. "Cam Hayward had one last year that got tipped in the end zone and got picked. So, they have a special feeling for it, and they've done a lot in their careers of making plays, pass rush, and pass breakups. So, it can't be something I'm really thinking about. They're going to try to get their hands up.

"I think just finding good passing lanes and moving around the pocket in some different ways. But really, I think it's easy to say quick game, but at the same time, they know they're going to get their hands up fast. So, it's just being cognizant of it, whether it's technique or little things to get the hands down."

The Patriots have released multiple players with injury settlements over the last few weeks, but only in three of six cases have they actually agreed to pay a settlement sum. According to a report by salary cap expert Miguel Benzan, only offensive lineman Andrew Rupcich, defensive tackle Isaiah Iton and safety Eric Butler were financially compensated:

OL Andrew Rupcich: $94,167 (3-week salary)

DT Isaiah Iton: $28,611 (1week salary)

S Eric Butler: $143,506 (5-week salary)

Players released by a team with a settlement are allowed to return after an agreed-upon settlement period. This means that, theoretically, all six could come back to New England at some point.

For the second time over the last six months, TreVeyon Henderson was in the headlines because of a social media post. When asked about it this week, however, head coach Mike Vrabel came to the second-year running back's defense.

"I think he's handled it maturely, and I think he tried to explain himself," Vrabel said. "TreVeyon Henderson is a special person, a great teammate. I love being around him. I think he's pretty much spoke on what he thought and what he believes, and I think that that's impressive for him to be able to speak on it. I'll leave it up to him."

The Patriots will host the Steelers at Gillette Stadium for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff on Sunday. From there, they are in their typical regular season mode.

This means Mike Vrabel media availability on Monday, off-day on Tuesday, and three straight practices plus injury reports from Wednesday through Friday. The team will then hold a final walkthrough on Saturday before traveling to Jacksonville for a 1 p.m. ET game with the Jaguars.

title: FINAL: Kansas State 31, Tulane 20
description: Avery Johnson and Jaron Tibbs eviscerated the Tulane defense in Kansas State’s win.
fullText:
A first-half struggle turned into second-half dominance as Kansas State rode a career day by Jaron Tibbs and the best performance of the year by Avery Johnson to roll to a 31-20 victory over the Tulane Green Wave on Saturday at Bill Snyder Family Stadium in Manhattan.

Johnson accounted for 379 yards of offense between his arm and legs, and Tibbs set career highs in both catches and yards. The Wildcat defense finally bent, giving up two touchdowns, but they forced Tulane (1-2) to eat a lot of clock in the process.

K-State (3-0) won the toss as well as the opening drive, forcing a 3-and-out. But the offense stalled, and the Cats had to punt. On Tulane's second drive, the Wildcat defense finally had a breakdown, giving up a 41-yard pass from Kadin Semonza to Oliver Mitchell as well as a pair big runs before Semonza scored on a nine-yard run. It was the first touchdown surrendered on the season by the Wildcat defense.

Another fruitless drive by the Cats was followed by a huge tackle for loss by Gabe Powers on a blown running play which led to a punt giving K-State decent field position. A 33-yard connection between Johnson and Tibbs and an 11-yard jet sweep by Brandon White got the Cats down to the four-yard line, but on the next three plays the Cats lost a yard. Luis Rodriguez came on to kick a 23-yarder to get K-State on the board at 7-3.

After two 10+ yard runs, an Elijah Hill sack led to a Tulane punt. Johnson picked up two first downs with his legs, then completed two big passes to Tibbs and Will Anciaux to get down to the Tulane two-yard line. Two plays later, Jay Harris bulled in to give the Cats a 10-7 lead.

Tulane went 3-and-out, and after an incompletion Johnson broke free down the sideline for 66 yards, then scored from seven yards out. Tulane ran the two-minute drill well until Jayden Bryant plowed Semonza for a loss of 13 on a third-down sack, and Tulane had to settle for a 58-yard field goal attempt by Cooper Helmke — which would have been good from 70. The Cats killed the final 17 seconds and took a 17-10 lead into the locker room.

After the break, K-State methodically moved downfield, eating up over eight minutes. The biggest play was a 27-yard completion to Anciaux, and Harris capped things with a one-yard run. Tulane responded, aided by a pair of concurrent penalties which erased a 21-yard gain by DJ Dugar; a late hit by Mekhi Mason resulted in 15 yards instead. Tulane got down the the 24, but a 1-yard stop, a 5-yard loss, and a 7-yard sack pushed them back to the 35 and a 4th-and-21. Helmke pounded a 53-yarder to bring the score to 24-13.

As the third quarter ended, on 4th-and-inches at theWildcats' own 34, Collin Klein opted to punt and rely on the defense. It paid off with a 3-and-out, and a 14-yard catch by Tibbs plus a 25-yard run by Johnson got K-State into the red zone. Johnson ran it in from 12 yards out a couple of plays later for a 31-13 advantage.

Tulane got a 22-yard gain on a pass play, then three plays later faced 3rd-and-19 but were bailed out by a pass interference call on Kaleb Patterson when Semonza was nearly sacked by Koy Beasley. Inside the 30, Bryant got his second sack of the day, but then on 3rd-and-17 Semonza found Maurice Turner for a 25-yard score to get within 31-20.

Tulane tried an onside kick, but K-State recovered, and after a first-down pass to Garrett Oakley after Tulane had exhausted their final time out, Johnson knelt the clock out for the win.

Johnson was fantastic today after a couple of shaky starts to begin the season. He was 21-28 for 227 yards although with no touchdown passes, and had a career-high 152 yards on 12 carries with two scores. The rest of the team only accounted for 49 yards on the ground, although with two touchdowns courtesy of Jay Harris.

Tibbs set career highs in both receptions (9) and yards (114). The tight ends were busy as well, with 4 catches for 27 yards for Oakley, 3 for 59 for Anciaux, and 3 for 23 for Linkin Cure.

K-State outgained Tulane 428-260, 201-95 on the ground and 227-165 in the air. Both teams were penalized five times, although K-State lost 34 more yards as a result than the Green Wave. There were no turnovers, and K-State led time of possession 33:41-26:19. The biggest eye popper on the stat sheet: Johnson was not sacked, while the Cats got to Semonza six times, and had 12 tackles for loss for a total of 64 yards.

Johnson was able to get yards himself, but the rest of the stable struggled today. Tulane was well-prepared, and the Cats are going to have to address that issue in conference play or things could get hairy.

They didn't get gashed horribly — in fact, on paper it looked like another great performance. But Tulane was able to get decent chunks and used the run game to move the chains often, and subtracting sack yardage like sane people do makes the numbers look a lot worse.

Semonza's numbers through the air today will be the cause of nightmares… for him.

Tibbs was mostly the invisible man in K-State's opening pair of games, but he was Johnson's favorite today. He had career highs in both receptions and yards, and while he didn't find the end zone himself he had a big part in every Wildcat touchdown today.

Cure caught 3 balls on three targets, presented a threat in the run game although he had no carries, and was on the field for most of the game. I think we can stop clutching our pearls.

Johnson had his best game of the year, but when you have a career day we're giving you the nod here. So Jaron Tibbs gets the nod this week. On defense, Will Gregory was once again great — three tackles for loss and half a sack — but we'll spread the love around and give it to Jayden Bryant and his two sacks and two TFLs this week.

The Cincinnati Bearcats come to Manhattan to open conference play in an evening game on ESPN2.

title: Latest impressive defensive performance helps undefeated Cedar Ridge stuff Rouse
description: After allowing nearly 40 points per game last year, Cedar Ridge's defense has dominated so far this season. The Raiders are 4-0 for the first time since 2017.
fullText:
Hours before Cedar Ridge's homecoming game Friday night against Rouse, defensive tackle Jeremiah Passmore promised himself that he was going to record a sack.

"Just manifesting," Passmore said of the self-made vow. "Got to manifest every game because last year I didn't really get to play at my full potential."

The 6-foot-3 lineman netted 1½ sacks, a forced fumble and three tackles for loss at the Kelly Reeves Athletic Center, as the Raiders defeated Rouse 34-16 to move to 4-0 on the season for the first time since 2017, when Cedar Ridge won a district title.

Friday marked another dominant performance for Passmore in a season in which the senior has been a mainstay of the Raiders' drastically improved defense.

"Our energy, we've really come together as a team," Passmore said after the homecoming triumph. "Everybody wants it. Everybody wants to get stops and stuff like that. We've really come together as one unit."

Cedar Ridge's 2025 campaign ended one win short of making the playoffs and with a defense that allowed just shy of 40 points per game. As the season slipped away and opponents kept stacking points, Passmore, who holds an FBS offer from Florida Atlantic, admitted that he mentally checked out.

"I wasn't really getting a lot of TFLs, I wasn't as dominant," he said.

MORE: Round Rock vs Vandegrift score: Dragons win high school football shootout

But things changed when the program brought on Brian Gaylor as its defensive coordinator. The hire of Gaylor, whom Passmore credited with his success this season, helped Passmore shed last year's failures and fully commit to maximizing his final year. The new coordinator has aided a drastic leap in Cedar Ridge's defense, which has allowed 20 points per game thus far, cutting its number from last fall by almost half.

"(Defensive) linemen really make it to where the (line)backers only have to worry about one gap," said linebacker Ayden O'Brien Brown, Cedar Ridge's leading tackler. "The front seven is playing really well together."

Behind the front seven, the Cedar Ridge secondary is thriving. The Raiders have intercepted seven passes this season.

A consistent defense has complemented an explosive offense. After averaging just over 36 points last season, Cedar Ridge is scoring 41.8 points this year, which includes a 21-6 season-opening win against East View that was ended at the half due to weather.

"We talk about a get-it-back mentality on defense," said Bryan Vardeman, the team's second-year head coach. "Our job is to get the ball back for the offense as fast as possible, and give them as many opportunities as we can."

On Friday, against a Rouse squad that had scored 100 points in its previous two games, Cedar Ridge's defense gave its offense plenty of opportunities.

MORE: Anderson football vs Lockhart final score: Trojans cruise to third-straight win

After allowing Rouse to march 80 yards and score on the opening possession, the defense shut out its opponent until the end of the third quarter. In that time, Cedar Ridge scored 27 unanswered points via Dylan Snoga's two first-half touchdown passes and third-quarter scores from running backs Tyler Mutz and Devin Patterson, who recovered a Mutz fumble near the goal line and ran it into the end zone.

After Rouse cut the lead to 27-14 at the end of the third quarter, it began the fourth by intercepting a pass at the Cedar Ridge 32-yard line. But Cedar Ridge caught a break on the next play, when a trick-play touchdown that would have cut the lead to one possession was negated due to a holding penalty.

On the next snap, Passmore broke through Rouse's offensive line and sacked quarterback Chase Whitten, forcing a fumble that was recovered by his linemate TJ Daniel near midfield. Eight plays later, receiver Terrez Harrison evaded multiple tacklers on a 3-yard score on an end-around - his second touchdown of the night - cementing a win that sends Cedar Ridge into District 25-6A play next week against Westwood unbeaten.

Passmore and the Cedar Ridge defense are eager to prove that the unit's performance through four weeks isn't a fluke in district competition, where it will battle regional powers Lake Travis and Westlake.

"We just got to play with a chip on our shoulders and just really, really physical," Passmore said. "That's really it - every drive."

As Vardeman prepared to be interviewed after the game, he spotted Passmore talking with his family.

The coach walked over, and standing next to the star defensive tackle, said, "We're proud of him. He knows that."

fullText:
A fundraiser for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who favored convicting Lindsay Clancy in her closely watched Massachusetts murder trial, has passed $300,000 on crowdfunding platform GiveSendGo.

The 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse was charged with three counts of first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of her children—Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan—at the family's Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. She pleaded not guilty.

Her defense attorney argued that postpartum psychosis had left her not criminally responsible for their deaths. The 12 jurors deliberated for seven days but failed to reach a unanimous verdict, leading Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial.

"I didn’t have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present," Desronvil said in a statement previously provided to Newsweek via his lawyer. "Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

In a statement on Friday on X, GiveSendGo co-founder Jacob Wells said he had spoken with Desronvil and his attorney Edward Paltzik.

“The Lone Juror is being added to the campaign as the recipient. His identity has been verified,” Wells wrote. “Thank you all for your generosity to this campaign.”

In a written statement on X, Paltzik thanked Wells and the fundraiser’s organizers for ensuring that all proceeds would go directly to his client to help pay for necessities after what he described as “death threats, doxxing and harassment.”

He wrote that “Stand With the Juror” would continue as the official and authorized fundraising page, with further updates to be posted there. Paltzik also thanked Wells for his leadership of the fundraising platform and acknowledged others who helped establish and support the campaign.

As of early Saturday, the fundraiser had raised a little over $330,000 of a stated goal of $350,000.

Newsweek reached out to Clancy’s attorney for comment via email on Saturday.

Desronvil, 48, from Massachusetts was the only juror who favored finding Clancy criminally responsible at her murder trial.

His attorney described him in a statement on social media on Thursday as an “American Hero and Champion of Justice [who] loves the United States of America as the greatest country in the world.”

Paltzik added Desronvil was “presently safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location in a rural area of Northern New England.”

Newsweek previously reported that court records showed Desronvil faced a criminal charge in 2021 for allegedly assaulting his then-wife to which he pleaded not guilty, and the charges were later dismissed, meaning he was not convicted.

Following the mistrial, the case remains unresolved and the murder charges against her are still pending.

The next confirmed court proceeding is a September 29 status hearing in Plymouth Superior Court before Sullivan. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, has filed a renewed motion asking the judge to enter a required finding of not guilty. He argued that the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence to establish criminal responsibility for the killings beyond a reasonable doubt.

Reddington has also said he intends to argue that another prosecution should be barred on double-jeopardy grounds, challenging whether there was sufficient necessity to declare the mistrial.

fullText:
US President Donald Trump signed a bill on Friday authorizing new sanctions designed to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine, after Congress gave its approval after months of delay.

Washington is pushing to revive a mediated path towards ending the conflict as Moscow intensifies attacks against Ukraine, even though much of its attention -- and munitions -- are focused on the ongoing war against Iran.

The legislation, which US lawmakers approved this week, takes aim at Russia's energy and defense sectors, alongside President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials.

It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to evade Western sanctions, and allows Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

That could potentially cover China and India, and furthers efforts to cut off revenue financing Moscow's war.

The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package by a 262-159 vote on Wednesday.

The bill would also target companies and foreign actors supporting Russia's military, and extend sanctions involving Iran.

But the broad powers to impose tariffs sparked an unusual split among Democrats, who largely support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump wider authority over trade.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier hailed the legislation as "symbolic" and thanked US lawmakers.

The bill is "an extremely powerful tool that can stop this terrorist war and bring Russia to the point where it has to make peace," Zelensky wrote on X.

"Sanctions must be strong so that all efforts for peace -- including our joint diplomatic efforts with the United States, Europe, and our other friends -- can succeed," he added.

India said on Thursday it would continue buying oil "through diversified sourcing."

New Delhi -- which counts Russia as one of its most important strategic partners -- has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran conflict in part by turning to Moscow, despite pressure from Western countries.

Supporters of the legislation argued that tougher economic pressure is needed against Moscow, which launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The Congress vote was celebrated by pro-Ukraine activists, who pointed to continuing Russian attacks, including drone strikes on Wednesday on civilian transport in the south that officials in Kyiv said killed five people.

Trump has generally preferred to retain control over sanctions and tariffs rather than have Congress dictate policy, helping delay the measure for more than a year.

The president's signing of the bill comes a week before he is due to meet with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington.

title: Kirb Herbstreit offers flimsy defense for ESPN's decision to interview Ted Cruz on College GameDay
description: ESPN committed a bizarre broadcasting faux pas last Saturday, by giving Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) an extended platform on College GameDay to push for the passage of the so-called Protect College Sports Act (which also could be called the Screw College Players Act or, as Simms suggested, Protect the ESPN and SEC Contract Act).
fullText:
ESPN committed a bizarre broadcasting faux pas last Saturday, by giving Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) an extended platform on College GameDay to push for the passage of the so-called Protect College Sports Act (which also could be called the Screw College Players Act or, as Simms suggested, Protect the ESPN and SEC Contract Act). The story has resonated throughout the week, and it looms over Saturday's episode of College GameDay in Oxford, Mississippi.

Kirk Herbstreit, one of the College GameDay analysts, addressed the situation in comments with reporters on Friday.

"I was first really impressed," Herbstreit said, via Mississippi Today. "I've never seen a guy booed that long and be able to just power through that. You know, I don't know if he could hear what I could hear, but it was pretty — I think he was booed pretty much the entire time he spoke.

"I don't really get into politics. It's just not — I'm kind of an independent guy, right down the middle of the fairway. I'm for America, so whoever helps us as a country, I'm for. Whether it's somebody on the left, somebody on the right, so I don't really follow it. I don't know anything about his political views. I don't know what he's for or against. I care about football, my family, and my faith, and my country. Those are things I love.

"And so, I don't really pick sides, and I was surprised. I didn't know what his deal was, so him being booed, I asked people, 'Like, what's going on here?' And we had him on because they were gonna be voting this week, and maybe he could give us some insight to what's going on. That was really it. So we're not picking sides in any way at all. We just want to see the chaos that's surrounding this sport kind of be reeled in, and if this will help us get to that, then great. Now, the fact that the guy that sits right next to me, Nick Saban, was heavily involved in putting this act together, this guy loves college football more than anybody I've ever met. And so if he's happy about what this could do, then I follow his lead. But yeah, that was surprising. But, again, I don't really follow it, so I didn't really understand it."

There's a lot to unpack there. I'll keep it simple. Herbstreit is either flat-out lying or he's ridiculously naive.

How can anyone say "I love my country" while being completely detached from the issues that shape its present and future? How can any American adult not know what it means to be a Republican or to be a Democrat, and how those labels have become so inherently polarizing and conducive to negative reactions?

Beyond Herbstreit's claim that he's clueless as to why someone like Ted Cruz would be booed, Herbstreit's position that he's "right down the middle of the fairway" and that ESPN isn't "picking sides" on the issue at hand can't be reconciled with his viewpoint that the "chaos" needs to "kind of be reeled in" and that he supports anything Nick Saban recommends on the matter because Saban "loves college football more than anybody I've met."

It's entirely possible to love college football and to want to limit player pay and mobility. Which is precisely what the Screw College Players Act will do.

The word "chaos" is a matter of perspective. From the players' perspective, it's not chaotic; they have real rights and power. From the perspective of those who don't like the fact that the rabbit has the gun, it's definitely chaotic. Because the rabbit has the gun.

The best news is that folks seem to be figuring out what's going on here. The powers-that-be don't like the fact that they've lost some of their power, given the implosion of a system that was fueled by antitrust violations that collectively prevented players from getting paid. In the aftermath of the reckoning, those who don't like the new reality are shedding crocodile tears and screaming "the sky is falling" to anyone who may be able to help them implement a system that limits the new rights the players enjoy.

It's a grift. It's a scam. Herbstreit has made himself part of that scam while pretending to be neutral — and not even his dog will shield him from the criticism he now deserves.

title: Washington football generating elite havoc rate on defense
description: The Washington Huskies have been among the nation's best at generating havoc plays on defense.
fullText:
Throughout fall camp, defensive coordinator Ryan Walters had one clear message when it came to improvements he wanted to see made on his defense: create more havoc plays. Just two weeks into the season, Washington's defense has wasted no time doing so. The Huskies are currently tied for No. 3 in the nation in turnover margin while ranking amongst the top teams in the country in havoc rate.

While the term "havoc rate" can be seen as a general statement to have an increased sense of intensity and urgency as a unit, there are analytics to back it up. The statistic refers to a defense's ability to create negative plays for opposing offenses, including tackles for loss, forced fumbles, pass breakups, and interceptions.

According to CFBTrack, the Huskies currently rank as the No. 4 defense in the country with a havoc rate of 27.8 percent, meaning they are creating a negative play approximately once in every four snaps. Washington trails only New Mexico, Virginia Tech, and LSU.

"We've been opportunistic for sure as a program," said Walters during Tuesday's press conference. "Not just as a staff, but as a program, we've definitely put an emphasis on generating takeaways and taking care of the football, so our offense has done a great job of not turning it over. So that's why were where were at, and we've taken advantage of opportunities to get takeaways, and so hopefully that trend continues throughout the course of the season."

One of the main contributors to the cause has been the defensive line, made up of a healthy rotation of veterans, transfers, and freshmen. On the interior, fourth-year Elinneus Davis has emerged as a leader in a group that features transfers Kai McClendon, DeSean Watts, and Darin Conley. That list doesn't include one of the most impactful new pieces of the line, freshman Derek Colman-Brusa, who has recorded 7 tackles, 2 for loss, and a sack in his first two games.

On the outside, starting edge rushers Jacob Lane and Ramzak Fruean have been a force to be reckoned with, but they're not the only ones wreaking havoc in the backfield. Fifth-year seniors Russell Davis II and Isaiah Ward, both of whom dealt with injury last year, have returned to play in a major way.

Davis tallied a sack in the Apple Cup, while Ward has recorded a tackle for loss to go along with a forced fumble and fumble recovery against Washington State. Now that both veteran Arizona transfers are healthy, Washington's pass rush has seen a massive leap in production from years past.

Him @AMcLaughlin28 ☔️ pic.twitter.com/3cEBh6YG9Y

To go along with a sturdy front seven is a secondary that flies to the ball, highlighted by safety Alex McLaughlin and freshman cornerback Jeron Jones. Through the first two weeks, the Huskies' back line has combined for five interceptions, with McLaughlin being responsible for a pair, Jones having one to his name, while Rahshawn Clark came up with the game-sealing pick against Utah State.

As Walters and his unit prepare for Eastern Washington ahead of Big Ten play, it will look to stay consistent in their ability to stifle opposition while creating extra possessions for an offense that has struggled so far.

fullText:
He was the sole holdout on a 12-person jury who otherwise voted to acquit Lindsay Clancy of murdering her three children — frustrating the defense and causing a mistrial.

After seven days of deliberations, and with specific instructions from Judge William Sullivan to follow the letter of the law on reasonable doubt, the jury said it still had one holdout who refused to budge. A mistrial was declared on Sept. 4.

Now, the lone juror, named Michael Desronvil, has come forward to share his side of the story, saying that he "didn't have any doubts" that Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

In a statement shared with Yahoo News on Sept. 18 by his attorney Edward Andrew Paltzik, Desronvil said: "I didn't have any doubts. As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented.

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned."

Desronvil refused to acquit Clancy on charges of the murder of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, whom she admitted killing in 2023.

Paltzik said in a social media post on Thursday that he was representing Desronvil and that his client would not be giving any interviews.

"We are focused entirely on his health, safety, and well-being," Paltzik said. "There will be a time for accountability and a time for the real story of the Lindsay Clancy Trial to be told. But not right now."

Paltzik added that his client was "safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location in a rural area of Northern New England."

The trial centered on whether Clancy could be held legally responsible for their deaths, as her defense argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time.

The case is scheduled to return to court on Sept. 29.

Desronvil's statement follows a number of jurors giving their views publicly about the case.

Last week, one juror said that Desronvil, one of three men serving on the jury, did not cite "a single piece of evidence" to support his position.

Juror Nick Dargie said the holdout juror did not show the other jurors any witness testimony or evidence to support his position.

"There was several times I would ask him to show us evidence or, you know, describe a witness testimony that helped to prove what he was saying, and ... he couldn't," Dargie said in an interview with ABC News aired on Sept. 10.

"There wasn't a single piece of evidence or witness testimony that he used to prove why he was thinking the way he was," Dargie continued, explaining that this was why the jury had given a note to Judge William Sullivan that eventually led to a mistrial.

"Otherwise, like, there's nothing wrong with somebody having a completely opposite opinion ... that would be a hung jury. That, like, that is our justice system."

Prior to Dargie's ABC interview, jury foreperson Roni Carlson had told NBC10 Boston that the holdout juror blocked Clancy's acquittal despite having reasonable doubt.

A guilty verdict requires guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the highest standard of proof in the U.S. legal system.

"He had reasonable doubt. He admitted he had reasonable doubt," Carlson said.

"I started filling out the forms, I was so excited. There were three forms I had to fill out, and then he said, 'But I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity.'"'

Another juror, who chose to remain anonymous, told local CBS station WBZ-TV that most of the jurors were "very firm in their stance," adding that "the stand-alone juror was not the only one that was unwilling to see things from the other side".

"I'm going to kind of defend that individual in a sense," she told WBZ-TV. "There were some big personalities in that room. But at the end of the day, it just came down to an inability to move past your convictions."

She added that there was "so much doubt."

"The prosecution didn't have a figurative smoking gun. There was not a single moment throughout the presentation of that case where you could say 'Yup, 100% I'm certain she did it' or that she didn't do it. There was too much gray area."

The two sides in the case are scheduled to return to court on Sept. 29, when the next steps will be decided.

Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not announced whether he will seek to retry Clancy.

Speaking outside the courthouse on Sept. 4 following the mistrial, Cruz said, "I appreciate the fact that there are strong feelings and opinions tied to this case."

He added: "However, our job is to set aside our feelings and focus solely on the facts. The facts are, Lindsay Clancy killed her three children and the evidence suggested to us that she was in control of her actions when she committed those homicides."

Meanwhile, Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, said he was open to a plea deal, but told CNN's Anderson Cooper that he would not agree to one that would result in her serving prison time.

"I want to hear what Tim [Cruz] has to say," Reddington said. "I hope, however, after sitting through this trial and seeing the evidence that was presented from the government, as well as from the defense, that he would revisit that issue."

WASHINGTON, Sept 17 (Reuters) - The Pentagon is reinstituting a mandatory testing program ‌for testosterone deficiency among US service members ‌age 30 and older, a spokesperson said on Thursday, ​bringing back a program that many medical experts have described as unnecessary and potentially harmful.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has promoted the use ‌of testosterone to ⁠improve military readiness, first announced the screening mandate in July.

Under the announced guidance, ⁠women were also set to be screened through a questionnaire and could then move to ​treatment for ​conditions related to hormonal ​imbalances.

In early September, ‌however, the Pentagon temporarily rescinded the published medical guidance for the testosterone screening "to allow for updates."

The latest move lifts that pause, allowing testing to go forward. It was not immediately clear what, ‌if any, updates had ​been made to the original ​policy.

"Effective immediately, this ​guidance addresses male testosterone deficiency, establishing ‌uniform screening and treatment ​pathways," Pentagon spokesperson ​Sean Parnell said in a statement.

Medical professionals have warned that testosterone, if prescribed inappropriately, ​could increase ‌service members' risk of infertility or lead ​to other health consequences.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Tensions are mounting between the Pentagon and Congress over the flow of information to lawmakers about the U.S. military's priorities, with both Democrats and Republicans accusing a Defense Department leader of being frustratingly opaque.

Some senators from both parties say they were left deeply unsettled Thursday after the Pentagon's top policy adviser, Defense Undersecretary Elbridge Colby, failed to provide an expected update on the Trump administration's National Defense Strategy at a classified briefing.

The lawmakers also say they were unsatisfied with Colby's answers to questions ranging from inquiries about the Iran war to growing concerns that President Donald Trump could deploy troops to polling places during November's midterm congressional elections. Colby acknowledged that discussions about deploying the National Guard were taking place.

Sen. Jacky Rosen, a Nevada Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said Colby "was not forthcoming" and "did not really address our concerns or issues."

Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican also on the committee, described the classified briefing as "just sort of dodge and punt."

"It's very peculiar to have somebody come in for a congressionally mandated update and not have a statement," Cramer said.

Colby, who has supporters and detractors on Capitol Hill, was expected to provide a required briefing on the National Defense Strategy, a comprehensive document that provides guidance for the military. Released in January, the blueprint reinforces Trump's "America First" philosophy of favoring nonintervention overseas and questioning decades of strategic relationships with allies in Europe.

Under the annual National Defense Authorization Act approved by Congress, he was required to provide the Senate Armed Services Committee with the classified briefing on implementation of the strategy no later than Sept. 15.

"It was not what we had expected," said Sen. Mike Rounds, a South Dakota Republican on the committee.

"Let's just put it that way," he said. "They owe us a report, and we did not get the report."

Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said he was able to ask about the strategy for the Iran war in Iran and the decision-making that has left the U.S. with what he described as a "munitions deficit." Experts say military contractors will need about three years to replenish stockpiles of certain advanced weapons, such as defensive missile interceptors.

"You walk out with more questions than when you went in, and for me, that was the case today," Kelly said.

At one point, Colby was asked directly if he ever had any discussions about deploying the National Guard for voter security on Election Day. He told senators that he had heard about some of those discussions taking place but that he wasn't leading on the issue.

"Never once said 'yes' or 'no,'" Cramer said.

The idea of deploying troops has been gaining attention as the midterms draw closer. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., recently pressed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, to confirm that they won't send troops to polling places.

Caine responded to Slotkin in a letter last month that said there are "no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections."

Colby did not receive criticism from all lawmakers who attended Thursday's briefing.

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., called it a "constructive, substantive" briefing that "answered all my questions."

Asked if he was satisfied with the briefing, Sen. Roger Wicker, a Mississippi Republican who is chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he would not be answering questions about the classified session.
