title: Cam Ward presents another dangerous mobility test for Eagles' defense
description: Philadelphia must pressure Cam Ward without creating the same escape lanes Jayden Daniels exploited during the season opener
fullText:
The Philadelphia Eagles spent part of Monday correcting the problems Jayden Daniels created outside the pocket. Their Week 2 opponent presents a similar concern.

Cam Ward combines high-level arm talent with enough mobility to punish undisciplined pass rushes.

Ward completed 19 of 32 passes for 140 yards and one touchdown during Tennessee's season-opening loss to the New York Jets. He also rushed four times for 21 yards, showing his ability to escape pressure and extend possessions. Defensive coordinator Vic Fangio praised Ward's arm strength, athleticism, and continued development under Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll. Philadelphia understands the challenge after Daniels hurt the defense with his legs, particularly during Washington's final two possessions. Fangio specifically identified quarterback scrambling as one reason the Eagles struggled to close the game.

The Eagles recorded one sack and did not consistently win their individual pass-rush matchups. When pressure arrived, defenders occasionally created escape lanes by losing rush-lane integrity.

A good portion of the #Titans passing offense required Cam Ward to create outside of the pocket, between facing quick pressure, lack of open receivers, or bailing the pocket. #Eagles D-line will have to be discipline in their pass rush lanes to prevent big plays from happening… pic.twitter.com/wRLLPPjt0p

That cannot happen against Ward.

Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith Jr., Arnold Ebiketie, and Philadelphia's other edge defenders must pressure from controlled angles. Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo must also compress the pocket without letting Ward escape through interior gaps. Tennessee allowed three sacks and scored only 10 points in Week 1, giving Philadelphia's rush a chance to improve. Pressure alone, however, will not be enough. The Eagles must finish plays. If Ward escapes the initial rush, he possesses the arm strength to find Calvin Ridley or Carnell Tate after coverage begins to break down.

Philadelphia's defensive plan must balance aggression with discipline.

title: Could Rams' exciting undrafted rookie get a shot with Myles Garrett out?

Myles Garrett barely practiced with the Los Angeles Rams this summer after being acquired in a blockbuster trade in June, and he won't be on the field for the next month, either. Garrett is being placed on injured reserve after undergoing knee surgery, sidelining him for at least four games.

Fortunately, the Rams have good depth at outside linebacker, starting with Byron Young and Josaiah Stewart. Sean McVay loves what both players bring, and he also mentioned Desjuan Johnson as someone who will step up, but what about undrafted rookie Wesley Bailey?

On the "Coach McVay Show" Monday, host J.B. Long brought up Bailey's name to McVay, and the Rams coach called the rookie someone who the Rams are "going to be counting on."

"He's another guy that we're going to be counting on," McVay said. "Whether that's making an impact on teams, whether that's continuing to understand the roles and responsibilities dependent upon which grouping we're in. Where is the role and responsibility that he's playing? He's another guy that'll be asked to step up, for sure."

Bailey was active in the season opener, which was a feat by itself as an undrafted rookie, but he didn't play any defensive snaps. That was with Garrett available, but now that the reigning Defensive Player of the Year is out, perhaps Bailey will get a greater opportunity.

He was a standout performer in the preseason, racking up 10 pressures in the second game against the Saints. He had five tackles, a sack, a forced fumble and four QB hits in the win, which all but secured his spot on the initial 53-man roster.

Bailey is a terrific athlete with elite length, coming in at 6-foot-4 with 34-inch arms and 4.69 speed at 260 pounds. Athleticism and measurables aren't everything, but he has the tools and frame to be a quality edge rusher in the NFL.

Young, Stewart and Johnson will get the bulk of the snaps with Garrett out, but in time, Bailey could get opportunities to rush the passer if he impresses in practice.

title: Russia readies new 500-mile missile as weapon expert warns of 'terminal end game surprises'
description: Russia plans to test a new 800-km ballistic missile by year's end, with an analyst warning its advanced maneuverability could strain Ukraine air defense.
fullText:
Moscow is preparing for a final test of a new ballistic missile capable of striking targets hundreds of miles away and potentially maneuvering in ways that could challenge Ukraine's already strained air defenses, a defense analyst warned Monday.

The warning comes as Ukrainian military officials said that Russia could conduct the test in the coming months and potentially in live-fire strikes.

"According to our estimates, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 km by the end of this year," Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), said at a meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, according to Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

"If, for instance, this 800-kilometer missile has more advanced maneuverability, well then that's going to create greater problems for Ukraine in that they're going to need the more sophisticated interceptors to get them," Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital.

Russia Deploys North Korean Missile Unit To Ukraine; Moscow-pyongyang Axis Deepens: Report

"This means terminal maneuvers that weave a little bit so that the defender doesn't quite know where it's going or what trajectory it will have," Karako said.

"Another possibility is that they just figured out a way to make some kind of 800-kilometer missile more cheaply or in large numbers," the expert said of the Russians.

Karako said developments in precision-guided munitions, along with a broader shift away from unguided weaponry, could offer clues about the type of missile Russia will launch.

Next-generation Missile Defense At Mission Speed

"Everyone is going for increased maneuverability," Karako explained. "Just about every gravity bomb that we have has some kind of terminal guidance for precision," he said, specifically of the U.S. arsenal.

"In a similar way, a moment's not too far in the future where you don't really have that many purely ballistic missiles."

"You have things that may be ballistic for a good part of their path, but are also equipped with maneuvering reentry vehicles or some kind of terminal end game surprises," he warned.

Meanwhile, according to Ukraine's DIU, Russian forces may try to strike targets in western Ukraine during the missile tests as a live-fire demonstration, which Karako said is standard practice in wartime.

"This is a business-as-usual arrangement where you might do lots of developmental testing and then formally field and then have your operational testing," the expert said.

Russia Unleashes Nearly 600 Missiles And Drones On Kyiv In Deadliest Strike Since May

"There are all kinds of norms being broken, though, because it is, after all, wartime, and so it may well be the case that some of this stuff is tested — maybe not the first time — but some of the early tests are done, frankly, in the field in Ukraine," he added.

The missile would, however, fall into a category once prohibited under the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, Karako warned.

Signed by President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev in 1987, the INF Treaty required the United States and the Soviet Union to eliminate ground-launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometers (roughly 310 to 3,400 miles).

The United States withdrew from the treaty in 2019 amid alleged Russian violations.

"This range is one that was formerly prohibited by the INF Treaty that capped ballistic and cruise missiles at 500 kilometers in range," Karako said.

"To some extent, you see Russia filling that gap, which is understandable and reasonable. Of course, they were violating the INF Treaty, which was why the United States got out of it."

Pentagon Plots New Nuclear Options For Trump As America's Biggest Adversaries Raise Stakes: Report

Missiles and artillery have been central to Russia's campaign against Ukraine since the start of the war in 2022. Ukrainska Pravda reported Aug. 10, citing Ukrainian military intelligence, that production of Russia's primary missile types had reached between 110% and 120% of monthly targets.

According to the Kyiv Independent, Russia fired at least 1,858 missiles of various types at Ukraine from the start of 2026 through Aug. 27.

"This is what's hitting Ukraine on a daily and weekly basis. And so it's in that broader context of that demand for standoffs of various kinds that you see new things pop up," Karako said.

Russia Threatens Strikes On Uk Military Targets, 'Catastrophic Consequences' Over Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy highlighted the growing strain on air defenses in an interview with Deutsche Welle at a Canadian military base in North Bay Sept. 12.

"I want to have 100-120 [interceptor missiles] for these difficult months, especially the cold months," Zelenskyy said. "We'll see how many months this winter lasts — that is, these cold months: one, two, three. We don't know. This is truly a major challenge."

"It is the case that Russia really is on a wartime footing, and they really have mobilized their defense industrial base to be cranking these (missiles) out like sausages," Karako said.

"There was a point in which everything was going to the front, everything was going to Ukraine."

"There have been other reports more recently that suggest that Russia may be keeping some in reserve," Karako added.

"There are lots of worries. If you're in Poland, if you're in Romania, if you're in the Baltics, you're worried about the Russians."

title: It's same ol', same ol' with Cowboys defense as hype gets pushed aside by reality
description: The Giants had the ball three times in the second half.  New York was 9 of 10 on third down for the game before Jaxson Dart's kneel-down on third down on the final play.  Receivers ran free in the secondary, just as they did a year ago when the Cowboys gave up the most points with the fewest interceptions in franchise history.
fullText:
FRISCO, Texas (AP) — Same old Dallas defense.

Even with a new defensive coordinator — the youngest in franchise history in 34-year-old Christian Parker — and an overhaul of the roster, the Cowboys were just as bad as a year ago in a season-opening 28-20 loss to the New York Giants on Sunday night.

Maybe worse, if that's even possible.

The Giants had the ball three times in the second half. They had two eight-minute touchdown drives, then ran out the final 5:21 on the third possession. New York was 9 of 10 on third down for the game before Jaxson Dart's kneel-down on third down on the final play.

Receivers ran free in the secondary, just as they did a year ago when the Cowboys gave up the most points with the fewest interceptions in franchise history. The run defense was porous in key moments — just as it has been for years now.

There was so much hype about the arrival of Parker and first-round draft pick Caleb Downs. So much hype about the Cowboys sticking to the business of football in the offseason while avoiding the soap operas that often surround them.

Hype has been replaced by reality with the home opener set for Sunday against Washington in a matchup of NFC East rivals trying to avoid an 0-2 start in the division.

"Don't flinch," coach Brian Schottenheimer said when asked what he would say to Parker. "You're going to get humbled at times. It happens. He'll learn from it. We'll learn from it. He's going to be hardest on himself anyways, he and the defensive staff."

Schottenheimer went off on the young players, unleashing an expletive while trying to explain why Dallas simply didn't cover running backs in the flat, repeatedly.

"Those are going to happen, and we have to coach the young players better," Schottenheimer said. "But when you play young players, it's part of the deal, and they need to learn quickly."

While Dak Prescott led the offense to touchdowns the only two times the Cowboys had the ball after halftime, his interception on an attempted throwaway late in the first half was the most pivotal moment in the game. New York scored touchdowns on either side of halftime because of it, breaking a 7-7 tie.

One of the problems the defense posed a year ago was giving Prescott and company little margin for error. Prescott wasn't buying talk of a 2025 replay, though.

"No, they did a hell of a job on the other side," Prescott said. "I'm in this year, sorry."

The Cowboys mostly matched the Giants with third down efficiency. Dallas was 8 of 11. The first of the three failed conversions came on the first series, when George Pickens caught a slant for what appeared to be a first down before replay assist turned it into fourth-and-inches. Schottenheimer elected to punt, making it a three-and-out.

The Cowboys had one game last season when both CeeDee Lamb and Pickens failed to reach 50 yards receiving. It was the meaningless finale against the Giants when both played less than 50% of the snaps. Lamb did have a touchdown among his 44 yards on Sunday night. Pickens finished with 28 and had a huge drop on a deep throw four plays before Prescott's critical interception.

CB Cobie Durant, who led the NFL with three interceptions in the playoffs last season, is making a case to be a full-time player. He was in on 72% of the snaps and had the only pass breakup among defensive backs while also forcing a fumble.

RB Javonte Williams had little impact — until his taunting penalty on the last Dallas touchdown when he held the ball out toward an opponent as he crossed the goal line. Schottenheimer said he planned to go for the 2-point conversion to try to get Dallas within six. Instead, Brandon Aubrey missed the 48-yard PAT try.

Schottenheimer said safety Malik Hooker may have fractured a forearm, which would mean two starters and a key backup are already on injured reserve just a week into the season.

The Dallas defense entered Monday last in the NFL in Week 1 with an expected points allowed per play of 0.34. Even Carolina was better at 0.33, and the Panthers lost to Chicago 59-37. A year ago, one of the worst defenses in franchise history finished at 0.13 expected points allowed per play.

The Cowboys haven't opened with consecutive losses since 2010, when Wade Phillips was fired midseason with a 1-7 record as Dallas went on to finish 6-10.

fullText:
No, it wasn't against a top ranked defense. And no, it wasn't against a P4 conference opponent. Nonetheless, Jayden Mandal put some doubts to rest on Saturday night about him being capable enough to be Fresno State's starting quarterback.

Mandal went 23-for-26 for 316 yards and two touchdowns, and a rushing touchdown, in the Bulldogs' 49-3 victory over Sacramento State. A stark contrast from his opening week performance against USC, where Mandal was 7-for-15 for 77 yards and an interception.

The junior gunslinger was responsible for the first three touchdowns for the Bulldogs, all of which came in the second quarter.

Mandal first found Speedy Luke for an 18-yard touchdown. He then followed that up with a 73-yard connection to Ezekiel Avit for another score, before using his legs on a quarterback sneak from 1-yard out to make it 22-0 Fresno State.

"I'm really excited for the young man," head coach Matt Entz said following the contest. "He had some people make plays for him. And he did a really good job of orchestrating the offense."

After a rough first outing against the Trojans, many fans and "pundits" wanted to see Fresno State's second-string quarterback getting some reps. Aside from Mandal's numbers, he was also responsible for a few of USC's points as he was sacked twice for safety in the loss.

However, Entz stayed the course with Mandal, stating that it was inexperience for Mandal and that a change now would cause him to lose the team. That vote of confidence for Mandal and his talent paid off for the Bulldogs on Saturday night. And now with the offense relying on both the pass and run games, the Dawgs have a shot to turn things around and perhaps become a contender for the College Football Playoff.

Mandal will now lead Fresno State into San Jose next Saturday night to clash with the rival Spartans for the Valley Trophy. That game is at 8 p.m. Pacific Time and will be on Fox Sports 1.

title: Why a certain WWE-style belt means Alabama football defense is at its best
description: After Luke Metz did his job, the Alabama football linebacker got to celebrate.
fullText:
LEXINGTON, Ky. — After Luke Metz did his job, the Alabama football linebacker got to celebrate.

Trailing by a touchdown in the first quarter against Kentucky, Metz was tasked with reading quarterback Kenny Minchey. Once Minchey threw, Metz stepped in front of the receiver, snagged the ball and ran it 34 yards for a touchdown.

From there, Metz got a chance to participate in a tradition Alabama has continued for years into this new Crimson Tide era: a WWE-style belt that celebrates takeaways. Once Metz got ahold of it, he called it "surreal."

"You want to get a picture with the belt," Metz said. "That's the goal."

When Alabama's defense is at its best, that "turnover belt" is being passed around. And in Saturday's 45-17 win against the Wildcats, the belt had its share of wearers with three forced turnovers: an interception and two fumble recoveries.

But Alabama doesn't need a belt or any evidence of a job well done. To linebacker Caleb Woodson, takeaways or crazy stat lines is just evidence of Kane Wommack's plan coming to fruition.

"Swarm D is going to the ball every play," Woodson said. "Whenever 11 bodies are out on the field, 11 bodies (are) getting to the ball, trying to affect the game."

Along with three turnovers, Alabama's defense allowed just 10 points and 209 yards. In the second half, Kentucky had 62 yards, three first downs and no points.

Through two games, Alabama's defense has allowed 20 points. Opposing offenses have converted one third down on 23 tries.

"Our defense did a good job of continuing to evolve throughout the game," Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer said, "but I thought we had a pretty good plan, a pretty good handle on things from the get go."

To defensive lineman Devan Thompkins, that success stems from trust of Wommack's calls and trust that his teammates are all in step with one another.

"We just went out and played our brand of football," Thompkins said. "That's what got us to where we were."

title: MSU defense show flaws without Jordan Hall, but return imminent
description: Jordan Hall missed Michigan State football's 35-7 win over Eastern Michigan with a right elbow injury, but he could play next week at Notre Dame.
fullText:
EAST LANSING — Michigan State coach Pat Fitzgerald thinks he may have his most important defensive player back for next week's game against Notre Dame.

In his postgame press conference after a 35-7 win over Eastern Michigan on Saturday, Sept. 12, Fitzgerald said that starting middle linebacker Jordan Hall was not cleared for the game by medical personnel but could be available for Week 3's rivalry game in South Bend.

"Jordan was really close playing today," Fitzgerald said. "Medical team told us that he was not cleared here late in the week. We made that decision collectively together to make sure that we think about his health, safety, and well-being. And I expect if we practice tomorrow that he'll be ready to go."

Hall made 88 tackles last season to lead Michigan State's defense and is a two-time captain. The senior made four tackles in 25 snaps in Week 1's win over Toledo but came on and off the field with a right elbow injury sustained on the second drive of the season. He walked into Spartan Stadium on Saturday with a brace on that right arm.

MSU LB Jordan Hall with a brace on his right elbow as he takes the Spartan Walk. 

Saw him wince on a couple of handshakes. We’ll see how he looks in warmups.@detroitnews pic.twitter.com/qklOKEfVbs

Without Hall, Michigan State leaned on linebacker Brady Pretzlaff to be its green dot — the player who communicates with defensive staff with helmet comms — and played a mix of Dion Crawford, Caleb Wheatland and Cam Stodghill next to him in a number of 4-2-5 and 4-3 looks. Fitzgerald said there is work for MSU's defense to do without Hall from a communication standpoint.

Pretzlaff credited Hall with preparing him to deliver on Saturday, when his eight tackles tied safety Devin Vaught for the team lead.

"I think Jordan himself has been a great leader throughout this week," Pretzlaff said. "It's hard for a guy like that who has played so much and is so passionate about the game to go down, and he's done a great job of himself kind of taking on the coaching role and getting us ready and kind of taking that role forward. So it's been great to see that, and I think our preparation really helped us attack it today."

More: Gaylord's Brady Pretzlaff proving MSU coaches' investment was worth it

The Spartans are 29-49-1 all-time against Notre Dame, which is ranked No. 4 in the USA Today Coaches Poll. In the past seven meetings dating back to 2009, Michigan State is 2-5 with an overtime win. Having Hall back will be important for Michigan State going into South Bend.

"Jordan's a huge piece of our program. He'll go down in Spartan lore when his career is said and done," Fitzgerald said. "So I don't want to minimize not having that big of a fixture of our defense out there, but it's next-man-up mentality, and those guys that went out there, I think learned a lot throughout the course of the game. I thought they played much better in the second half, and we need to continue to reinforce those guys playing that way."

Saturday, Sept. 19's game comes 60 years after Notre Dame ran out the clock against Michigan State in 1966's "Game of the Century," a 10-10 tie that led to both teams sharing pieces of the national championship that year.

Michigan State hasn't played Notre Dame since Sept. 23, 2017, when it lost 38-18 at Spartan Stadium.

title: Cleveland Browns DC Mike Rutenberg: ‘We’re arriving with bad intentions’
description: Cleveland new man in charge of the defense has a clear idea of what he wants from his side of the ball.
fullText:
The Cleveland Browns will sport a new defensive look when they take the field on Sunday for their Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Some of those changes are by design: defensive end Jared Verse replaces Myles Garrett, linebacker Quincy Williams replaces Devin Bush, and defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg takes over for Jim Schwartz.

There were some unexpected changes, however, most notably along the defensive line, after defensive end Alex Wright, who was expected to be a starter, was lost for the season to a torn Achilles tendon.

That led general manager Andrew Berry to bring in veterans Sam Williams and Derek Barnett, and Rutenberg to experiment with Michael Hall Jr. at defensive end.

Rutenberg had his weekly press conference on Thursday and addressed several topics. Here are four takeaways from what he had to say.

There are no bigger shoes to fill for a defensive player than those of Myles Garrett, who picked up his second Defensive Player of the Year Award in 2025 after bagging an NFL-record 23 sacks.

Garrett is now with the Los Angeles Rams, while Verse is in Cleveland and bringing his own style to the defense, according to Rutenberg:

"(Jared's) such a unique guy. He's really like a unicorn in that he sets a standard with his play style and who he is. Really, what we saw early is what we continue to get. He sets that standard from the jump, in meetings, great questions, great insight. And then on the practice field, his standard of not only performance but style, and how hard he plays, has been the same every day. It's really cool to see."

Adding veterans is nice, especially for a team that is in the second year of a youth movement, but adding them so close to the start of the season is not always ideal. Especially with everyone on the defense already working with a new defensive coordinator and not necessarily able to quickly bring the new guys up to speed.

But so far everything has gone smoothly with Barnett and Williams, according to Rutenberg:

"It's awesome to get new guys. The nature of this league is that you get new players, and those guys have worked as hard as you could possibly imagine. They've worked their butts off. Derek's obviously been in it. Sam's had experience in it. Those guys are pros, man. They approach it the right way. We've got a great defensive line coaching staff, starting with Jacques (Cesaire), Ralph (Street), Laroy (Reynolds), Shaq (Wilson), and together they're preparing really hard. It's really cool to see."

finding a way to win on defense@GetSpectrum | #DawgPound pic.twitter.com/pREF2cg2NZ

All through training camp and the preseason, Rutenberg has talked about how "the ball is oxygen," and the defense needs it to survive. He also wants his defense to have a very particular mindset when it takes the field:

"When the ball is thrown, we're arriving with bad intentions. We're built off that. We choose violence in everything we do, and it doesn't have to be a tackle; ball's in the air, we're knocking it out. That's what we're built off. We do our job so my brother can do his; I do mine and a little bit more. And our guys have done that. They do it in practice; they do it in walk-through. It's awesome to see.

"I'm excited to watch us play as hard as possible. I can't wait just to watch us celebrate together. I can't wait to see our preparation hopefully come to life. We're built off violence, and that's what we're looking for in every play."

Far too often, fans and media focus on sacks and turnovers as the only sign that a defense is successful. Those are fun, no doubt, but pressuring a quarterback into a bad throw is just as helpful. And turnovers are not something that a defense can control.

For Rutenberg, however, there is only one clear goal:

"Win. Win. I want to help the Browns win. I learned that from Jeff Ulbrich, man. Raheem Morris used to say, 'help the team win on defense. Find a way to help the team win on defense.' It's a team game; we're a team staff, Browns helping Browns, man. I want to help this team win."

title: How LB Brady Pretzlaff fulfilled promise of Michigan State football D
description: Brady Pretzlaff missed most of last season after a shoulder injury. The sophomore is now a starting linebacker for Joe Rossi's Michigan State defense.
fullText:
EAST LANSING – Jeff Pretzlaff stood in the stands, watching his son, Brady, dash onto the Spartan Stadium field for his return to college football.

The challenge of a long year and injury recovery was behind the Michigan State football linebacker. A coaching change had given the younger Pretzlaff a new start and some impactful new mentors. And an important one still remained.

Most impressively, the travel travails of Joe Rossi years earlier – through the snow of Up North – had paid off with a connection that remains strong as Brady emerges as a starter for the Spartans.

"Just seeing him back out there, there was just so many feelings that would describe it," Jeff Pretzlaff said Thursday, Sept. 10. "I was just so happy for him. Just to see all that hard work that he did, to now get it back. For me personally, I was just blown away. Like, oh my gosh, it's just crazy to see my son playing in front of 80,000 people out there."

SCOUTING THE GAME: Who to watch in Michigan State vs EMU

Brady, a third-year sophomore, had career highs with five tackles and 44 snaps on defense in MSU's 30-20 opening win over Toledo on Sept. 4, his first game action since suffering a season-ending shoulder injury against Youngstown State on Sept. 13, 2025.

Almost a year to the date of having football taken away from him, Pretzlaff is lined up for his second college start when the Spartans (1-0) host Eastern Michigan (1-1) on Saturday (3:30 p.m., Big Ten Network).

The 6-foot-3, 238-pounder credited MSU's medical and training staff for his recovery and called it "a long buildup" to finally get back to playing the game he loves and learned from his father, who is the defensive coordinator at Gaylord and played at Augustana College in Illinois.

"Honestly, just a grateful feeling in those first few plays, just taking it all in," Brady said Wednesday.

Back when Mel Tucker was coach at MSU, the Gaylord native initially committed to play for Rossi and P.J. Fleck at Minnesota in January 2023. Then Tucker was fired that fall. And when Tucker's replacement, Jonathan Smith, hired Rossi as defensive coordinator with the Spartans in December that year, Brady quickly decommitted to join them.

The relationship between the Pretzlaff family and Rossi began with multiple recruiting trips from Minneapolis to Gaylord. On one of those visits, Rossi's two-wheel-drive rental van, picked up after a flight into Traverse City, got stuck in a snow-covered Gaylord parking lot in the dead of winter.

"It's kind of like a fishing story," Jeff said with a laugh. "We've kind of embellished it over the years."

UNDER CONTROL: Michigan State football wants aggressive, not reckless defense

Rossi and Brady both smiled about that memory as well after the younger Pretzlaff joined Jordan Hall as MSU's starting linebackers against Toledo.

"I think it was great experience to get him out there," Rossi said Wednesday. "I saw him in pregame, and I said, 'Dude, remember when I made, like, five drives up to Gaylord?' And I was at Minnesota at the time. I said, 'It was with the intent for you to be a Big Ten starting linebacker.' And he got an opportunity to do that here at State."

Jeff, while he was coaching at Big Rapids High, got his son playing football in third grade. Brady also ran out onto the field during his father's games, grabbing the tee after kickoffs. Jeff also had Brady playing basketball and baseball year-round, but football naturally was the best fit and progressed as they moved to Gaylord, where Brady became a three-star recruit.

"I think the small town just has a different level of grit to it to a certain extent," Brady said. "The amount of support I've had from the town of Gaylord, it's been huge to me. … And to be able to perform for my family and for them, that means a lot to me. That's something that I take with me when I'm going to compete."

It's a career path, from Up North to East Lansing, similar to that of Brady's new position coach and co-defensive coordinator, Max Bullough (who starred in Traverse City). And along with having Rossi's tutelage, getting to play under another former All-American in Pat Fitzgerald – who retained Rossi when he was hired in December – has given Brady a graduate-level lesson at linebacker.

"I couldn't even draw it up myself any more perfectly," Jeff said of the Spartans' stacked staff of linebacker knowledge.

MSU's first-year head coach said he believes Pretzlaff is not even scratching the surface of how good he could be."

"Brady, I think, is just going to be an absolutely outstanding linebacker in this league," Fitzgerald said Monday. "He can do it all. He's physical in block destruction, he can play the pass, he can rush the passer, he's one of our best special teams players. I think the game – and I don't want to speak for him – but my opinion, watching the way he works, having the game taken away from him, has highly motivated him."

Brady said he relied on his family, his faith and his teammates – including leaning on Hall – to get through the arduous rehab with his shoulder and being limited during spring practices. Yet even after going through preseason camp and getting the nod against the Rockets, he felt concerned about how it would be to hit someone full speed again after the injury.

"But something I learned is once you're out there and get that first crack of the pads, it's really like riding a bike," Brady said. "It all comes back to you."

The sensation of that first tackle against Toledo ultimately "felt great," he said. Brady also wants to restore something else – the type of aggressive, physical defense he watched Bullough and the Spartans play while he was growing up 2½ hours away.

"It's a physical ballgame, and Michigan State's a physical school," he said. "Being able to be able to hit there and do a live rep, I mean, that's what we do it for. That's a lot of fun."

description: Schematic brilliance and pre-snap disguises dismantled Sean McVay’s offense as San Francisco stifled Matthew Stafford, proving that tactical discipline outweighs raw pressure in high-stakes defensive domination.
fullText:
Coming into the season opener at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, all eyes were on how the San Francisco 49ers defense would manage the pass rush with Nick Bosa on a rotational snap budget (he ended up playing the entire game) and front-line depth depleted by injuries. But defensive coordinator Raheem Morris delivered an absolute masterclass in scheme execution, leading the 49ers to a dominant 27-7 victory over the Los Angeles Rams. While San Francisco didn't generate overwhelming pressure off the line of scrimmage, Morris had Sean McVay's high-powered attack completely solved from the opening whistle.

Rather than relying on raw pass-rush wins to rattle reigning MVP Matthew Stafford, Morris relied on schematic discipline, pre-snap disguises, and layered zones.

The 49ers took away the intermediate middle of the field, forcing Stafford into hesitant, late read checkdowns and contested boundary throws. Stafford was held to just 155 passing yards and spent the last three quarters completely shut down, managing only four completions in the first half as San Francisco erased Los Angeles' quick game rhythm.

Morris' defensive masterwork was capped by two defining situational stops:

The Goal-Line Wall: Late in the third quarter, holding a ten point lead, the Rams drove to the 49ers' 1-yard line. On fourth-and-goal, Stafford attempted a QB sneak, but Morris' front held the line, with Osa Odighizuwa and Keion White stonewalling the attempt for a massive turnover on downs.

Secondary Traps: Cornerback Renardo Green executed a flawless zone read early in the game, jumping a route for a leaping interception that set the tone for the secondary.

Later in the fourth quarter, All-Pro linebacker Fred Warner delivered the knockout blow, punching the ball loose from tight end Tyler Higbee to kill another Rams drive and preserve the double digit lead.

With Bosa's snaps carefully budgeted and new interior pieces integrating on the fly, Morris proved that elite defensive calling isn't always about blitzing high or generating backfield chaos. It's about taking away what the opponent does best, executing in critical high leverage moments, and dictating the tempo of the game.

fullText:
Stephen Aarons said he tried to use ChatGPT to create a ‘bulletproof summary’ during a murder conviction appeal

A defense lawyer appealing his client’s murder conviction submitted a legal brief containing ⁠made-up police testimony and ⁠witnesses fabricated by OpenAI’s ChatGPT, ​New Mexico’s highest court said.

The New Mexico supreme court on Wednesday fined the attorney, Stephen Aarons, and held him in contempt for failing to verify the accuracy of the court ⁠filing, which Aarons said he prepared with help from the artificial intelligence (AI) application.

The filing “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses”, the court said.

The panel also said Aarons had “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern ⁠for his client”. The justices fined Aarons $5,000 and said they will refer him to an attorney disciplinary board for investigation.

Aarons in a ​statement said he had used ChatGPT to summarize ‌the trial proceedings when he agreed ‌to take up the defendant’s appeal last year, and did not understand the degree to which AI could “hallucinate” facts.

“I am remorseful but ‌hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake,” he said. “It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.”

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The court’s sanction is the latest in a growing number of cases in which state and federal judges have disciplined lawyers for submitting court documents generated by AI tools without adequately vetting them. Some judges have also faced scrutiny over the use of AI themselves.

Dozens of lawyers ‌have been sanctioned for filing briefs in which AI made up case citations or misquoted the law. Aarons’ filing appears to have gone further, containing fabricated witness testimony in a criminal appeal.

Aarons, a private attorney based ​in Santa Fe, was handling the appeal of Oscar Renee Sandoval, who pleaded not guilty to the murder of the mother of his children before he was convicted and sentenced last year to life in prison.

The appeal is still pending and was assigned on 2 September to Kim Chavez Cook, a New Mexico public defender. Cook declined to comment. The local district attorney’s office also declined to comment.

The ⁠state supreme court last month ordered Aarons to explain how the fabricated material, which it said ​appeared to include “fictional statements that the shooter ​was wearing dark pants and a white shirt”, ​was included in his primary brief in the appeal.

Aarons told the court at an 21 August hearing ​that he fed a computer-generated transcript ‌and other case ​materials to ChatGPT, presuming it would ​generate “a bulletproof summary”.

The justices sounded incredulous that Aarons was not fully aware of how AI can make mistakes.

“Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world?” Justice Shannon Bacon said at the hearing. “Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an ‘above-the-fold’ story every single day.”

title: Michael Burry says the best defense against dollar doom and AI disasters might be a fine Bordeaux
description: Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame said fine wines can protect investors against dollar weakness, fiat flight, and "hellscapes" caused by AI.
fullText:
Michael Burry made the case for investing in fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday.

The "Big Short" investor said they're a "terrific diversifier" for portfolios.

Burry said fine wines could benefit from dollar decline, fiat flight, and AI fallout.

Michael Burry has turned from water to wine.

The star of "The Big Short," who made waves for investing in water after calling the collapse of the mid-2000s US housing bubble, explained why he's betting on fine wines in a Substack post on Thursday.

Burry, who pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments almost a year ago, told his subscribers that fine wines could be a "terrific diversifier" for their portfolios.

He wrote that "just about every single case of fine wine sitting in a London bonded warehouse can be a short position on the US dollar, a global hedge against fiat currency, and a ward against global financial systems' vulnerability to the various hellscapes possibly wrought by future iterations of AI and quantum computing."

Burry said that if new technologies threaten the digital financial system, the greenback "could accelerate its ongoing loss of reserve status to real assets."

One beneficiary could be fine wines, as the Liv-ex Fine Wine 100 index has been negatively correlated to the US Dollar Index across overlapping five-year periods, he said.

Burry said fine wines could function as a hedge against the "colossal train wreck" he expects for the dollar over the next five to 10 years, as the "bills of fiscal irresponsibility come due."

He was referring to the US national debt, which has roughly doubled since 2010 to a record $40 trillion, and the government's interest payments, which account for more than $1 trillion of its roughly $7 trillion annual budget.

Burry described how fine wines are highly differentiated and have a set drinking window, so "every bottle of wine consumed anywhere on earth shrinks the inventory of that exact asset forever."

"Supply destruction is both continuous and a bullish supply dynamic that spirits, watches, and art can never match," he added.

Burry pointed out that the finest wines — including Pétrus, Margaux, and Mouton Rothschild — cater to the ultra-wealthy, so they "inspire resilient demand in good and bad times."

However, their hefty price tags likely restrict this trade to investors who can afford to spend five figures on wines and have them only account for 10% or less of their portfolios, he said.

Burry, a value investor, said a key reason to buy into fine wines now is that prices have tumbled by around 25% to 30% from their October 2022 peak.

title: More than 500,000 Russian troops killed in Ukraine, UK defense chief says
description: More than half a million Russian troops have been killed in Ukraine since the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, a senior British defense official said Friday.  The dead are part ...
fullText:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — More than half a million Russian troops have been killed in Ukraine since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, a senior British defense official said Friday.

The dead are part of 1.5 million Russian casualties in Ukraine, Air Chief Marshall Sir Richard Knighton, Chief of the U.K's Defense Staff, said.

The U.K. figures roughly coincide with those published by the Ukrainian military. There was no immediate comment from Russian officials.

Moscow's bigger army is struggling to make headway on the battlefield. Western officials and analysts say the Russian rate of advance has slowed significantly this year.

Russia's armed forces have also lost an "enormous" amount of military materiel, Knighton told reporters. That includes more than 10,000 armored and protected vehicles, close to 3,000 air defense and artillery systems, and over 370 aircraft and helicopters, Knighton said.

He didn't say what Ukraine's losses were.

Neither Moscow nor Kyiv give regular updates on their battlefield losses.

Russian drones targeted roadside gas stations in Kyiv for a second straight day Friday, as Moscow broadened its air war in what Ukrainian officials say is an effort to rattle civilians.

The attacks struck two Ukrnafta gas stations, killing two people and wounding six at one of them, the prosecutor's office said.

Russian strikes on urban gas stations have intensified in recent months, mostly in regions near the front line in eastern and southern Ukraine. It is part of a campaign to disrupt civilian life and weaken morale that has also included attacks on food distribution hubs, sporadically leaving some supermarket shelves bare in the Ukrainian capital.

"Russia is systematically attacking places where it knows people will be spending their time going about their daily lives, seeking to maximize casualties, spread fear, and put pressure on Ukrainian society," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X late Thursday.

Authorities have urged residents not to linger near gas stations and other exposed infrastructure during air raid alerts.

Ukraine is urgently trying to improve its air defenses as Russia's invasion stretches into its fifth year, and on Thursday won pledges of more support from Canada.

Pavlohrad, a city in central Ukraine, observed an official day of mourning Friday for five residents killed near shopping malls in broad daylight by Russian drones the previous day.

The attack also wounded 67 people, Sybiha said on X.

In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, a 32-year-old woman and her 10-year-old son were wounded in an overnight Russian drone attack, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The drones struck a nine-story apartment block and a shopping mall, it said.

Efforts to put out the blazes were slowed by the constant threat of repeat strikes, forcing firefighters to stop working and take shelter, it added.

In Dnipro, a city in central Ukraine, a Russian daylight attack Friday wounded 12 people, according to local officials.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has extended its own long-range drone campaign deep into Russia, straining air defenses across its bigger neighbor's vast territory. On Thursday, its military reported hitting a refinery more than 3,000 kilometers (1,800 miles) away in Siberia as Kyiv tries to hurt Russia's vital oil sector. Its strikes have caused fuel shortages in Russia, one of the world's biggest energy producers.

Russia's oil product exports hit record lows in August, and Moscow is importing fuel from South Korea and India, the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air said in a report.

"Ukrainian strikes on Russia's refining capacity have turned tables on the world's once largest oil product exporter to see them start importing fuels, with imports surging to a record 172,000 metric tons (189,600 tons) in August — more than seven times the previous monthly high," the Finland-registered nonprofit said Thursday.

Ukraine launched a major barrage overnight from Thursday to Friday, with the Russian Defense Ministry saying air defenses intercepted 777 Ukrainian drones over 16 Russian regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the waters of the Azov and the Caspian seas.

Two people were killed and three others wounded overnight in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Tula region south of Moscow, local officials said Friday.

A Ukrainian drone strike during the night started a fire at the Saratov oil refinery in southwestern Russia, Russian independent online outlet Astra said Friday. Kyiv has repeatedly targeted that refinery, which was last hit in early August.

Major online retailer Ozon said its logistics facility in the same city was struck and set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone, though no casualties were reported. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said long-range strikes overnight hit eight Russian regions, including a business and an oil industry facility in the Saratov region.

The attacks were "aimed at reducing Russia's capacity to wage war," he said on X Friday.

Burrows reported from London and Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.

fullText:
The defense says: ‘It’s about competition, not conspiracy’

A US prosecutor described China’s Huawei as a criminal enterprise that stole from US companies to build its telecommunications empire, as ⁠the trial against the tech company kicked off in Brooklyn federal court on Wednesday.

“Theft, lies, cover-up,” Taylor Stout, a trial attorney from the US Department of Justice, said in the government’s opening statement. “For 20 years, that’s how Huawei, a massive Chinese telecommunications company, victimized American companies ⁠and abused the American financial system, all ⁠in an effort to dominate the telecommunications ​industry around the world.”

Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from five US companies, including operating system source code for internet routers from Cisco Systems and a robotic arm to test phones from T-Mobile, to gain an unfair competitive advantage and grow its business, ⁠the prosecutor told jurors.

“We’ll hear from people who caught Huawei red-handed trying to steal American tech,” Stout said, adding there was video of an employee stealing the robotic arm.

The defense painted a very different picture of the company and its success in court.

“It’s about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, ⁠not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct,” Brian Heberlig, one of a team of lawyers representing Huawei, said in his opening. “Huawei earned its success ... There was no blueprint for crime.”

Huawei is known ​for its telecommunications equipment, mobile phones and, in recent years, AI chips. It does ‌business globally but its networking gear is restricted in ‌the US and suppliers are banned from exporting US goods and technology to the company without approval from the Department of Commerce.

On Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said “the Chinese ‌government firmly opposes the US side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” when asked about the case and the US prosecutor’s “criminal enterprise” description.

China “firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests”, the spokesperson said at a regular press conference.

The case against Huawei began in 2018 with an indictment charging the company and its chief financial officer with bank fraud and sanctions violations for allegedly misrepresenting its business in Iran to get around US sanctions and move millions of dollars through the US financial system.

In the ensuing years, it grew into a sprawling indictment that includes racketeering, a pattern of illegal activity conducted by an enterprise to generate profit.

Heberlig, defending Huawei, told jurors that prosecutors will describe routine activities ‌by global tech companies “but will twist those ordinary activities to try to make them look criminal”.

He said the incidents involving Cisco and T-mobile were “actions by individual employees” and that ​management worked to make things right after learning of them.

The prosecutor also accused the company of keeping the nature of its work in Iran secret so it could launder US dollars through the financial system and could help the Iranian government spy on its own citizens. The defense said there was no evidence Huawei knew the dollar-clearing would violate US sanctions law.

In 2018, Huawei’s chief financial officer, ​Meng Wanzhou, was detained in Vancouver after being picked up on ​a US warrant as a part of the original indictment. She fought extradition for nearly three years before being freed to return to China ​in a diplomatic agreement between the US, China ‌and Canada.

The charges against her ​were dismissed in 2022 as part ​of a deferred prosecution agreement but admissions she made are set to be introduced as evidence at the trial, which is expected to last three months.

title: Abington football runs Longmeadow off the field in season-opening win
description: A key stop by the Green Wave defense and a potent rushing attack were the difference for Abington on opening night.
fullText:
ABINGTON -- Success came and went for Abington high school football in its 2026 season opener. But enough Green Waves were made to outlast its opponent.

After trading haymakers all night, Abington, a Division 6 program, delivered the final blow to Div. 4 Longmeadow 43-21 in the first game of the season at home on Frolio Memorial Field on Thursday, Sept. 10.

For most of the game the Green Wave outlasted a relentless Lancer team with its bruising and dynamic run game and an opportunistic special teams unit. But it was a defensive stand that sealed Abington's victory.

With 9:20 to play, trailing 35-21, Longmeadow had a fourth-and-goal from Abington's 1-yard line. The Lancers handed it off to 6-foot, 207-pound running back Maury Garrett lll, but he was stonewalled and driven back nearly eight yards for a turnover on downs.

The play kept Longmeadow from bringing it back to a one-score game. Abington's offense capitalized and finished a 91-yard touchdown drive with a 15-yard run by sophomore Jake Lehman for the game's final score with 5:29 remaining.

Abington's offense totaled 260 rushing yards on the evening. Five of the six touchdowns came via the ground game. Lehman had the highest rush total on the night, accounting for 84 of those yards and a pair of touchdowns. He scored Abington's first points of the season in the first quarter on a 24-yard scamper after Longmeadow scored on its first possession to go up 7-0.

Junior Daniel Pifer led the team in total offensive yards with 103 (68 rushing, 35 receiving) and two touchdowns. Senior Nazir Paulding tallied 57 rushing yards and had a 55-yard punt return touchdown for a total of 112 all-purpose yards and two total touchdowns.

Abington's offense didn't punt until the final drive of the game.

title: Ukraine says AI is moving beyond drones and into strike missiles for the first time

fullText:
Ukraine is developing artificial-intelligence-enabled missiles, a first as its autonomous warfare evolves.

Brave1, Ukraine's state-backed innovation platform, said multiple companies are part of this effort.

AI has already been widely incorporated into Ukrainian drones and robots.

Ukraine is developing strike missiles augmented by artificial intelligence, a first and a significant step as its offensive weapons become increasingly autonomous.

Brave1, the Ukrainian state-backed innovation platform, confirmed to Business Insider that multiple companies involved in this initiative are developing AI-enabled missiles.

Ukrainian companies have widely incorporated AI into their drones and war robots, enabling functions such as decision-making, navigation, and targeting. Missiles are new.

"AI was initially deployed at scale in drones," Andrii Hrytseniuk, Brave1's CEO, told Business Insider. "It's not that fast — it's sufficient for the drones, but missiles require much higher speeds."

Hrytseniuk shared that AI is now "increasingly being integrated into missile systems as well. Although it hasn't reached the scale of hundreds of solutions seen in the drone sector, we are already seeing first successes and plenty of developments in progress."

More than 200 Ukrainian companies were developing AI-based parts for missiles, drones, radars, and other systems, Hrytseniuk said in an earlier interview in May.

Efforts to integrate AI into missiles appear to have ramped up as Kyiv invests in developing long-range strike weapons, often used to attack military and energy targets inside Russian territory.

Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister who pushed for advances in battlefield innovation and just launched a high-profile venture fund in Kyiv to invest in military startups, said this week that one of his priorities is "low-cost strike missiles and, eventually, missiles powered by AI."

It's unclear how the Ukrainian companies are using AI in the country's missiles and how far along they are in the development process. The technology will add to Kyiv's capabilities, but won't remove humans entirely from the process, Brave1 said.

The approach echoes Ukraine's use of AI in warfighting systems more broadly. Both soldiers and defense companies have stressed that humans must remain involved in operations in some capacity, saying that drones can't act entirely on their own.

The war has become significantly more autonomous over the past year as Ukrainian and Russian drones flood the battlefield. They constantly monitor the front lines, creating a miles-wide "kill zone" where any movement could trigger a precision strike.

Ukrainian officials have set out to replace soldiers with ground robots and drones in particularly dangerous missions — such as casualty evacuation and logistics — whenever and wherever possible, reflecting the push to become more autonomous.

Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners

The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way.

“They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”.

The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power.

Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”.

“I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.”

It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform.

But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children.

Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability.

“The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

title: Ukrainian woman designing a ballistic missile to put Moscow in reach
description: Before Russia invaded, Iryna Terekh designed patios. Now she runs a Ukrainian defense company testing a missile she says will soon put Moscow in range.
fullText:
Kyiv — Ukraine's most important weapons manufacturer wears mismatched earrings and a black knit dress.

"The good thing about being the boss is that you get to set the dress code," Iryna Terekh, the 34-year-old CEO of Fire Point, one of Ukraine's largest drone makers, told CBS News, grinning as she took a seat next to a model of one of the company's latest designs.

With her high heels, bright smile, and entourage of millennial assistants and executives, Terekh stands out in her factory, where throngs of middle-aged men lug drone parts, wield power tools and chain-smoke cigarettes. But she is hardly an exception in a country forced to reinvent itself since Russia launched its invasion in February 2022.

"When the full-scale invasion started, a lot of people had to review what could be their personal impact," she said. "You never really know what kind of knowledge and what kind of experience could be transformed and pivoted into something new."

Terekh's experience was in design and management.

Trained as an architect in the northern Ukrainian city of Irpin, she started building patios and outdoor furniture while also developing a successful high-performance concrete company.

In the early months of 2022, Russian forces occupied Irpin, destroying roughly 70% of the city.

"I understood how vulnerable we are to the complete barbarian behavior of our enemy," Terekh told CBS News. "And if there are any competences that I could put on the table for the sake of fighting this war, then I have to do this."

After escaping Russian occupation, Terekh began looking for a way to help. In the fall of 2022, Russia started attacking Ukrainian cities with Iranian-made, long-range Shahed exploding drones. It also started manufacturing its own versions, known as Gerans.

Terekh and Ukrainian businessman Denys Shtilerman, whom she had worked with designing outdoor urban spaces before the war, decided to build their own long-range attack drones to help Ukraine strike back.

Shtilerman had a background in defense engineering, but most other initial members of the team, including Terekh, came from civilian backgrounds. Yehor Skalyha, their third co-founder, was a film producer.

At first, the company aimed to build 20 of its FP-1 drones per month. By 2024, they were regularly being used to strike Russian airfields, ammunition depots and oil refineries. But over the last two years, the company's ambitions, and its arsenal, have grown.

Fire Point now makes 300 to 400 long-range attack drones per day, and it has added more advanced weapons to its production lines.

In June, a Fire Point cruise missile completed a mission of over 1,000 miles, which she claimed as the longest-range strike ever carried out by a cruise missile in combat history.

Terekh also made the bold claim that Ukraine has launched twice as many deep strikes into Russia as Russia has into Ukraine in 2026 — with 60% of the Ukrainian attacks using Fire Point weapons.

She said her company is now just months away from deploying Ukraine's first domestically designed and manufactured ballistic missile. Unlike cruise missiles, which stay lower to the ground, ballistic missiles follow an arc trajectory that takes them much higher, making them harder to intercept.

Fire Point is among many Ukrainian startups that have helped to shift the country from being solely a recipient of military aid to an engine of defense technology innovation.

Many other companies have similar, unlikely stories of their beginnings. The founder of Sine Engineering, which has attracted American investment in its communications and navigation technology, ran a business making standing desks before the war. Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of the Fourth Law, which makes autonomous guidance systems for drones, previously founded Petcube, a pet tech startup backed by the American business accelerator Y Combinator.

Terekh believes these companies, with their founders' diverse backgrounds outside the defense sector and their shared ability to pivot to new endeavors, have been key to their successes.

"This works in Ukraine because we have very low bureaucracy, because we have direct communication with the army, and because we have companies that react," she said.

The country's innovative approach to defense manufacturing and procurement has also attracted the attention of its allies.

In 2025, the U.S. military announced its own program to copy Iran's Shahed drones, known as "LUCAS," which deployed its first relatively cheap long-range drones in the Middle East in February.

The U.S. and Ukrainian governments are expected to sign a new defense agreement soon that would expand Ukrainian military technology exports to the U.S. and joint ventures with American companies.

Terekh said Fire Point's primary focus remains on Ukraine's defense, but she welcomed the idea of one day playing a role in a new, wider Western security architecture.

"We need to ensure that Ukraine will stop just being a breadbasket for the world," she said, referring to the country's longtime primary export of grains. "Now we have something to offer which is much more valuable, and the defense industry is a huge driver for this."

title: Where can the Steelers rank top 10 in 2026?
description: The Steelers’ roster looks stronger than last year’s — could a top-10 finish on offense or defense be on the horizon?
fullText:
Top 10s have long been the standard of excellence when it comes to rankings, and in the 32-team NFL, it's a signifier of being in the top third of the league — not unachievable or elite, but above average in a game where even the smallest of margins can make a massive difference.

So, with the Steelers' regular season debut rapidly approaching this Sunday and predictions season starting to give way to actual football, let's take a look at where Pittsburgh could rank among NFL teams in the four main yardage metrics: passing, running, pass defense, and run defense. They're listed below based on how likely they are to land in the top 10 this season, from most to least.

Pittsburgh didn't finish as a top-10 team in any of these metrics in 2025. Could things change under a new coaching staff this year?

2025 finish: 13th in NFL; 113.1 rushing yards allowed per game

Why the Steelers will finish in the top 10: This is a deep defensive line that features the ageless Cam Heyward and a bevy of run stuffers including Derrick Harmon, Yahya Black, Sebastian Joseph-Day and even impressive rookie Gabriel Rubio. Pittsburgh's edge rusher room is better defending the run than many realize as well. The strong front should open things up for an athletic inside linebacker room that could finally live up to its potential in Patrick Graham's aggressive scheme. And for the most part, the Steelers' secondary isn't afraid to tackle, with names such as DeShon Elliott, Jaquan Brisker and Jalen Ramsey all being known for laying out big hits in the box.

Why they won't: The range of the Steelers' inside linebacker room is not a question, but communication and block-shedding issues have been a common theme of past seasons for Patrick Queen and Payton Wilson. Top backup Cole Holcomb still doesn't look like the player he was pre-injury, either. The defensive line also isn't without its question marks. Heyward still looked elite last year but is now firmly in his late 30s. And a lot of the optimism surrounding the group's depth is banking on some sort of second-year leap from Harmon and Black, which isn't a guarantee.

2025 finish: 29th in NFL. 243.9 passing yards allowed per game.

Why the Steelers will finish in the top 10: Pittsburgh boasts one of the deepest cornerback rooms in the NFL with an excellent projected starting trio in Joey Porter Jr., Jalen Ramsey and Jamel Dean (Killer J's, anyone?). Don't forget Jaquan Brisker, either, a versatile safety who should be a big improvement over the list of veterans the team cycled through last year. Pair that revamped secondary with a modern Patrick Graham scheme and star-studded pass rush, and the Steelers' passing defense has the pieces to take a big leap from its disappointing 2025.

Why they won't: Porter has barely practiced all summer and has hinted at a contract holdout. Ramsey will turn 32 this season. The starting secondary as a whole hasn't been the most available this summer and could still be gelling come Week 1. The safety depth chart could once again sink the defense, with a lack of range across the board and DeShon Elliott starting the season on injured reserve. There are a surprising number of factors that could go wrong.

2025 finish: 26th in NFL; 103.3 rushing yards per game

Why the Steelers will finish in the top 10: Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle are both 1,000-yard season-capable runners who give the Steelers one of the most underrated one-two punches in the NFL. The Zach Frazier/Mason McCormick duo should also be a powerhouse in the run game, and new head coach Mike McCarthy's more varied run scheme should give the team a more diverse ground attack that might better cater to some players' strengths. Keep in mind that tight end Darnell Washington might be the best run blocker at his position in the NFL, as well.

Why they won't: Warren and Dowdle are good but not superstars, and if the offensive line fails to generate enough push up front like what happened in the preseason, the team's running backs might not be able to create much yardage. Remember that the Steelers often needed to switch to a jumbo package or heavily use Washington last year to successfully run the ball, and the team will likely be using more 11 personnel in 2026. The right side of the Pittsburgh O-line doesn't have a ton of power, and the group as a whole was built for Arthur Smith's zone scheme, not a McCarthy system that uses more gap/power concepts.

2025: 22nd in NFL; 202.4 passing yards per game

Why the Steelers will finish in the top 10: Aaron Rodgers' arm is still remarkably strong even at age 42, and the Steelers revamped the team's wide receiver room entering 2026 with the additions of veteran possession receiver Michael Pittman Jr. and rookie Germie Bernard. Despite a down 2025, WR1 DK Metcalf is still an explosive player and should see a boost in a modernized passing game under McCarthy. The same could be said of tight end Pat Freiermuth, who has been underused in past seasons but could finally break out under the coach who jumpstarted the careers of Jake Ferguson and Dalton Schultz. Don't underrate Warren's ability as a check-down target, either.

Why they won't: Rodgers had a historically fast time to throw last season, which shouldn't change much in 2026 considering the team is still catering to his preferences, the offensive line remains a work in progress, and Rodgers is still in his 40s and not going to be running around extending plays like he used to. That quick passing game could lead to a strong completion percentage, but it also doesn't do much to create big plays. And beyond Metcalf, the passing game is severely lacking in more options to gain chunk yardage.

Do you think the Steelers will rank in the top 10 in any of the above categories in 2026? What other metrics could Pittsburgh rank especially high or low in? Join the BTSC community and let us know in the comments.

title: Philippines' Teodoro says China could exploit cuts in US-South Korean exercises
description: By Kyu-seok Shim SEOUL, Sept 7 (Reuters) - China could see recent cuts to U.S.-South Korean military exercises as an opportunity to reassert itself in the Indo-Pacific, Philippine Defense Secretary
fullText:
SEOUL, Sept 7 (Reuters) - China could see recent cuts to U.S.-South Korean military exercises as an opportunity to reassert itself in the Indo-Pacific, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said on Monday, though he said Washington had assured Manila that ‌its commitments to the Philippines remained unchanged.

Speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of the Seoul Defense Dialogue, Teodoro said there had been ‌no reduction in U.S.-Philippine military activities and that bilateral and multilateral cooperation involving Manila continued to expand.

U.S. President Donald Trump's decision last month to scale back military exercises with South ​Korea has prompted debate among security analysts over the credibility of U.S. deterrence in Asia and whether rivals such as China could perceive a weakening of U.S. resolve.

"It is a possibility, of course. China is very quick to exploit gaps," Teodoro said when asked whether Beijing could seize on the move.

"If we're talking about the Indo-Pacific as a whole, then it may signal some opportunity for China to reassert itself," he said.

Teodoro said, however, that Manila had received "definite ‌assurances" from Washington and that there was "no indication" that ⁠the changes in South Korea would affect commitments under the U.S.-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty.

Manila has deepened defence cooperation with the United States under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., including expanded joint exercises and greater access for U.S. forces to ⁠Philippine military facilities, as tensions with China have intensified in the South China Sea.

Teodoro said Manila was also broadening security ties with other partners. The Philippines recently concluded agreements with Canada and New Zealand, signed a visiting forces agreement with France, and was negotiating a similar pact with Britain, he said.

The defence chief also ​accused China ​of relying increasingly on influence operations alongside military and maritime pressure.

"Definitely it takes ​advantage of democratic space in order to co-opt people and ‌to use a free media to expand its distortive narratives," he said.

Teodoro said the Philippines was pursuing stronger espionage and foreign influence legislation to counter such activities.

Asked about Marcos' recent remarks that progress was being made toward possible joint oil and gas exploration talks with China, Teodoro struck a cautious note, saying it would be "doubtful" that any economic cooperation could be insulated from longstanding sovereignty disputes in the South China Sea.

Responding to Teodoro's remarks, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Monday that China "has always been committed to maintaining peace and stability in the Asia-Pacific region, refraining from ‌great-power confrontation, and hopes that relevant countries can also play a positive role in ​regional peace and stability."

Teodoro was in Seoul for talks aimed at expanding ​defence cooperation with South Korea, one of the Philippines' largest arms ​suppliers.

South Korea has supplied the Philippines with FA-50 light combat aircraft, frigates and other military equipment as Manila modernises ‌its armed forces.

He said the Philippines was interested in deeper ​industrial cooperation and emerging defence technologies from ​South Korea, but indicated that a long-discussed submarine acquisition programme remained some way off.

"The submarine program is still under review," he said, citing questions over mission requirements and the substantial infrastructure needed to support such a capability. "I would say it will be still a ​way off."

Teodoro said concerns about China's actions were encouraging ‌closer security cooperation among countries across the region and could ultimately lead to a more interconnected Indo-Pacific security network.

"I believe so ​because the motivating factor there is China," he said.

title: Phillies Former Outfielder Cut By New Team Shortly After PED Defense
description: The Philadelphia Phillies’ former outfield slugger has been cut from his new roster just a few days after offering an interesting defense.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies' brief relationship with a long-time big league outfielder came to an end before he could establish himself as a long-term piece in the organization.

After spending the 2025 season in Philadelphia, Kepler entered free agency and then immediately faced an 80-game suspension that dramatically complicated his attempt to find a new opportunity.

Kepler eventually landed with the Arizona Diamondbacks at midseason, giving the former Minnesota Twins regular a chance to rebuild his value in the majors. Instead, his return to the field produced another difficult chapter shortly after he spoke out at length about his PED suspension for the first time.

Yankees, Red Sox Castoff Left 'Crying' After Sudden Move To Another AL East Rival

Kepler's brief comeback has now ended with another roster setback. The Arizona Diamondbacks designated him for assignment and recalled catcher Adrian Del Castillo from Triple-A Reno on Sunday, Connor Byrne reported for MLB Trade Rumors.

Even before the suspension, Kepler seemed unlikely to re-sign with the Phillies as he struggled to consistently produce during his lone season with the team. He hit .216/.300/.391 with 18 home runs in 474 plate appearances, numbers that translated to an 88 wRC+.

The 33-year-old remained unsigned until June while serving the suspension that stemmed from his positive PED test. Arizona ultimately gave him a major league opportunity on a prorated contract but his return did not produce the rebound the Diamondbacks hoped to see as they push toward a playoff spot.

After being activated on June 25, Kepler hit just .205/.262/.303 with two home runs over 145 plate appearances, resulting in a 53 wRC+ and a career-low .098 isolated power mark.

Kepler also struggled against right-handed pitching, an area where he had traditionally been more productive. During his brief Arizona stint, he hit only .192/.256/.283 against righties.

Former Dodgers All-Star Slugger Sets HR Record With Latest Team

Kepler's recent explanation for the suspension added another layer to an already unusual stretch of his career.

"Our theory, which we were trying to put together with my lawyers, was the fact that you can consume a steroid with contaminated red meat, which I was eating a lot of red meat at the time," Kepler explained to Phillies Nation's Destiny Lugardo last week. "Then again, even if you would have sourced the contaminated red meat, there's no chance that a company admits to contaminating their meat. So this theory was a theory, but it wouldn't really hold up. So a positive test is a positive test."

While Kepler defended his positive PED test as unintentional, observers could be taking note that his production picked up notably in the latter part of last season and then appeared to drop off when he returned this season.
