title: Jon Sumrall praises offense, challenges defense after FAU win
description: Jon Sumrall discussed Aaron Philo's debut, Jadan Baugh's explosive performance and areas Florida must improve after its season-opening win over FAU.
fullText:
Florida football coach Jon Sumrall met with reporters following the Gators' season-opening win over FAU on Saturday night.

Sumrall evaluated Aaron Philo's debut as Florida's starting quarterback, Jadan Baugh's explosive performance and an offense that produced 66 points and 624 yards. He also praised Vernell Brown III, D.J. Coleman and the Gators' perimeter blocking.

The first-year Florida coach was less satisfied with his defense, saying the unit has plenty to correct despite the lopsided victory. Sumrall also discussed his first Gator Walk, running onto Florida Field and the importance of continuing to develop the team's younger players.

Here's everything Sumrall had to say.

Glad to be 1-0 and happy for our guys. It was fun watching a lot of our production tonight. I thought the guys came into the game with the right mindset and the right approach.

They were prepared. They didn't take the opportunity for granted. They were emotionally charged and ready to go. There is a lot to clean up. It was by no means a perfect performance. There is a long list of things we have to get a lot better at if we have high goals here.

I'm grateful for the fans. Unbelievable turnout and energy. It was electric. I got asked a little bit ago about running out of the tunnel for the first time. It surpassed my expectations, and I had pretty high expectations of what it was going to be like. What an unbelievable crowd and great support. They had a huge impact on the game. We need that each and every week, which I have no doubt we will.

I'm grateful for the guys' effort. There is a lot to work on and a lot to grow from. I told them just now that the journey of a thousand miles starts with a single step. That was step one. The goal this week was to be 1-0. We've got to go back to the drawing board and get a little bit better each day this week to keep improving.

I'm proud of him. He's prepared. He has worked really, really hard. He's an unbelievable teammate. He's a great leader. The game means a lot to him. I think he showed his comfortability by how he operated. He made good decisions for the most part with the football.

He was accurate. He distributed it well. I thought he did a really nice job. The interception really wasn't on him, to be quite honest with you. That ball should have been caught. I thought he played really well.

We're really young as a team. Jadan Baugh may not be young, but there were a lot of guys out there playing football who are just young.

I told the staff going into the game that we were going to be aggressive all night. We're not in any position to shut it down right now. We've got to figure out who the next guy up is and roll guys in. We weren't going to change how we played the game.

I'm very proud of Aaron. His preparation showed up tonight in how he played.

He had a little ankle injury. I don't know how severe it is. He tried to give it a go. We'll see. I'll probably have more information for y'all Monday. Unfortunately, it happened really, really early.

He's a really good football player. I tell Buster all the time, "Don't know what to do? Just hand it to 13. That will work, usually." He's phenomenal. He's a great kid and every bit as good as I thought he would be. I told him the night before the game, "Hey, I'm glad you're still here. Thanks for staying."

I'm very, very glad he's a Florida Gator. I love his playing style and demeanor. I also had a great appreciation for seeing his enthusiasm late in the game when he wasn't playing.

He was excited for his teammates to have opportunities and success when he saw Duke, Byron and some of the other guys in the room get carries. Rubio got in there. Seeing his excitement for his teammates says a lot about him, too.

Early on, we couldn't keep pace with them. Our defense was atrocious at times, quite honestly. We had a hard time keeping pace with them. I'll watch the tape, but I'm a little bit frustrated with how we played defensively at times.

I don't think we're as good as we think we are. I think we've got some guys who feel like we've arrived in some spots, and that will be addressed. We've got a lot of room to grow on defense.

If it doesn't happen really fast, we're going to get embarrassed and exposed pretty handily in some spots because that wasn't a great performance by us.

Hats off to FAU. They do some really good things. I love their quarterback. I played against the kid last year. I love the way he plays. He's tough, competitive and a leader. He's just a really good football player.

Zach does a great job offensively. Their offensive staff is really good at what it does, and they stress you out. That number eight, the little slot receiver, hit us on a slot fade. He's a good player. He averaged 12 targets a game last year for them. I'm sure he probably had about that tonight. I don't know how many he caught, but it felt like every time they threw to him, something good happened for them.

It was a good test. It was a really good test for a Week 1 game. They're a talented team, and I wish them nothing but the best.

It was a long day, but it was a great day. It was fun. A lot of fun. I tried to take in as much of it as I could, but at the end of the day, it's about winning a game. You're focused on what we've got to do to position ourselves to be successful on the field.

But all the great things around our program make this place what it is. The Gator Walk was unbelievable. When we left the hotel, there was a crowd of people in the hotel parking lot. I'm like, "All right, this is kind of cool. These people are waiting to see our guys walk to the bus at the hotel."

The support we have here is unbelievable, and I could not be more grateful for it. We're doing everything we can to make them proud. I'm very grateful for what Florida Gator Nation is all about.

It was fun. It was good. There was a lot of good in there and plenty of things to get better at. But I want our guys to have fun playing. I tell our team all the time that when you were growing up as a kid, you never said, "I want to go work football today." You always said, "I want to go play football." That doesn't mean it doesn't take hard work, but the work should be fun. Competing is fun, and making plays is fun.

The thing I'm most proud of tonight offensively is our perimeter blocking. Our receivers blocked their asses off. In the run game we created tonight, there were times on the perimeter when our receivers were competing to make blocks.

That says a lot about who they are. The character of a football player sometimes isn't revealed when he is getting opportunities for production. It's revealed by what he is doing to serve his team. I thought those guys blocked with edge and competitiveness.

That makes it fun. Competing is fun. I think it was a fun brand to watch tonight. We need to keep it up.

It was exhilarating. I was like, "All right, this is real." The energy in the stadium was — man, it was on fire. You could feel it. It was probably even better than I thought it was going to be. It was just really, really cool.

D.J. is one of those guys who is just really consistent. He's a high-level communicator. He has a high football IQ. He's smart, tough and dependable. I'm not surprised.

He showed it in the spring game. He had a pick on the glance route, and everybody was like, "Oh, the quarterback threw a pick." I'm like, "Well, that was a freaking unbelievable play that 33 made."

He's a really good player, and I'm glad he's on our football team. He has been a great pickup for us. He practices really hard every day. He invests a lot in his craft. He's just a steady, steady player. I'm not surprised by how he played because that's how he practices.

He had a big night. That was his first touchdown. I was getting on him all offseason. I'm like, "You haven't scored here. Everybody thinks you're this big-time player. We've got to see you score touchdowns."

To see him make the plays he made tonight — he had a couple of big plays. The first one was explosive. It was a great, great play by him. He's another unbelievable worker, so I'm not surprised. He competes his tail off and prepares the right way.

I'm happy for his success because he's one of the best leaders for a young player I've ever been around. He's a second-year player, a true sophomore, and he's a phenomenal leader and a great teammate.

That was good. He stuck his foot in the ground at the end of that run to get more and didn't just think the journey was over. I think he has taken on that challenge. We've challenged him with that sometimes on long, explosive runs.

I tell the receivers and the guys on the perimeter that an eight-, 10- or 12-yard run becomes a 40- or 50-yard run because they block better. They get on the safeties, and you're kind of nagging the defensive backs and getting in their way to create longer runs.

It was great to see him pop that long one. I'm proud of his performance.

Like I said, I thought our perimeter blocking was good. I thought certain guys on defense, at times, showed their contact courage. Maybe we weren't where we needed to be across the board, but I felt some physicality.

Procedurally, I'm probably most pleased with the offense. A lot of times in Game 1, there are delay-of-game penalties, illegal formations, false starts or a lot of other issues. It felt fairly clean in how we operated offensively.

Our special teams played really well. Durk hit the 50-plus-yarder. I think it was a 53-yarder. I thought he kicked the ball off well.

Other than the kickoff coverage where we missed a hit and didn't make the tackle, which I wasn't pleased with, I thought there were a lot of good areas.

At that point, I'm never going to be the one who tries to run up the score, per se. But I'm also not going to be someone who just shuts it down. Micah Jones scored the last touchdown, right? That was Micah, correct?

He is on the scout team all week right now. He's a young player who needs to improve for his own development and for our football team to continue growing. Byron Louis is kind of the fourth or fifth back right now, so I wanted to see him play.

I wanted to see Tramell operate and compete. I wanted to get Will Griffin in. If we had another drive, Will Griffin was probably going to go in. Those guys practice really hard.

At that point, I'm not saying, "Hey, we have to score again." If we score again, that's the nature of the deal. They were also bringing a lot of pressure. We had to get the ball on the perimeter and do some things because they were loading the box to stop the run late.

Those guys work incredibly hard all week. When their opportunities present themselves, we're going to let them play because we still have to develop those young players so they're more ready.

It was 1-0. That was the goal this week. We'll celebrate this a little bit tonight and then wake up tomorrow. We'll watch the tape, make corrections and then turn the page tomorrow night at about 5. Our staff meeting is at 4 tomorrow. As soon as that staff meeting is over, we'll watch special teams as a staff.

Then it's 1-0 and on to Campbell. It's about trying to win one game next week and focusing on that game all week. It's a good start. Being 1-0 was the goal this week, and we got there. Tomorrow at about 5, my mind will be 0-0 again.

It's just going into every game and focusing on one game at a time. It's coach speak, but that's how we operate.

Going back to it, we still need to figure out who we can rely on and who will be dependable. With the depth of our team, maybe on the line, there is still some room to figure that out. I wanted to see the backs go.

Rod Kearney came in. Caden (Jones) got in there, and Caden has started games before. He came in, and we need him to elevate his play. All those guys have to continue elevating. At offensive line, you have to get players ready to play because it's a long year.

You never know when their opportunity is going to come. You can't just think it doesn't matter whether he's getting better. We've got to get everybody in this program better. Everybody. Jadan Baugh has to get better. Everybody on our team has to continue getting better.

Those young linemen, Rod and Dice — Dice played some tackle that I liked. Those guys have to continue elevating so they can be dependable and reliable when their numbers are called.

Evan was available, but he had a little bit of a hip issue that wasn't feeling great. He didn't feel like he could do it. He was cleared to go but just didn't feel like he could push through it. I thought Duke did a really good job. London Montgomery is a good player back there, too. Byron Lewis did some good things tonight as well.

title: Texas Republican: ‘I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy’
description: Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally r...
fullText:
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense's argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children.

"I don't have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy," Gill said Friday on Fox News's "The Will Cain Show."

"I have an enormous amount of sympathy for the three little innocent kids who were slaughtered," he said earlier.

Gill went on to push back against the central argument of Clancy's defense: that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at the family's Massachusetts home in 2023.

"You don't get licensed to murder your children or anybody else just because you have mental health problems," Gill said. "We've gotten in a habit of medicalizing evil."

Trial Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when jurors remained deadlocked for seven days without being able to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

A last-minute attempt was made by Clancy's attorneys to remove the lone holdout juror, whom they accused of refusing to properly apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to remove the juror.

The legal battle has dominated national headlines, with even President Trump weighing in to respond to news of the mistrial.

"It's a shame. It's a horrible tragedy," Trump said when asked about the case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. "She did a horrible, horrible thing."

"I guess they're going to go through another trial. It's too bad," he concluded.

title: How integral to Bills defense line will Greg Gaines be in 2026?
description: Buffalo had been linked to a nose tackle from the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but they acquired his former teammate instead
fullText:
With a switch to an odd-man front on defense, the Buffalo Bills have been changing their defensive personnel throughout this offseason. In some ways, the team has had to be creative, asking players drafted for former head coach Sean McDermott's four-man defensive line to change their roles and body types in preparation for a season under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. In some cases, though, the Bills have gone outside of their usual comfort areas to find different player archetypes.

One of the more oft-discussed positions in the new defense has been that of the nose tackle. Buffalo didn't have a traditional nose tackle with McDermott given that they generally had two defensive tackles on the field at once, but players like DaQuan Jones and Star Lotulelei served roles similar to that which a nose tackle would traditionally fill in a three-man front. The Bills have an answer in the middle, but they definitely need depth at that spot.

In today's installment of our "91 players in 91 days" series, we discuss a veteran nose tackle ostensibly signed to provide said depth.
_____________________________________________________________________________

Experience/Draft:  7; selected by the Los Angeles Rams in the fourth round (No. 134 overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft

Acquired:  Signed with Buffalo on 8/18/2026

Financial situation (per Spotrac):  Gaines signed a one-year deal at the veteran's minimum. The total deal is worth $1,487,500, but thanks to the veteran's salary benefit, his cap hit comes in lower at $1,262,500 for the season. If Gaines is on Buffalo's Week One roster, his entire base salary ($1.3 million) becomes guaranteed thanks to his status as a fully vested veteran. If he's released prior to the start of the first game, Buffalo will carry a dead cap charge of $137,500 for the season.

2025 Recap:  Gaines once again served as a rotational nose tackle for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers last season, appearing on 35% of the team's defensive snaps across 17 games. Gaines offers little in the way of pass rush, so he mostly plays on early downs and in obvious run situations, acting as a gap-plugger and run-stuffer up front. He totaled 23 tackles, three tackles for loss, and two sacks last season.

Positional outlook:  Gaines is one of ten defensive linemen listed on the current roster. Ed Oliver, Deone Walker, Landon Jackson, Zane Durant, Phidarian Mathis, Zion Logue, DeWayne Carter, Travis Clayton, and T.J. Sanders are the others.

2026 Offseason:  Gaines has been a free agent since his contract with Tampa Bay expired at the start of the new league year. He has participated in practice and preseason action since signing with Buffalo.

2026 Season outlook: While he fills a need as a potential nose tackle, as Skarekrow pointed out in his All-22 analysis after Gaines signed, the veteran can play multiple spots along a three-man line. Tampa Bay frequently used him off center, and while that might have been because they had Vita Vea to plug the middle, it bodes well for Gaines' chances to come in and contribute along the line in Buffalo.

Behind Deone Walker, Buffalo doesn't have much going at nose tackle. Phidarian Mathis looked like a solid bet to make the team as the backup nose, but a three-game suspension for an alcohol-use issue while he was with the New York Jets means that he will begin the year unavailable. I guess being with the Jets could drive anyone to drink, but I digress. The Bills have also asked third-year man DeWayne Carter to bulk up and play the nose, and while he has done so, he hasn't exactly separated himself this summer, and after a weak rookie season followed by a lost second year due to a torn Achilles, it's not wise to assume that he can just come in and play at the level Buffalo needs.

Gaines, then, not only has a good shot at making the roster based on his experience alone, but I would go so far as to say he has a strong chance to carve out an important role on defense. Whether he's spelling Walker or playing alongside him on first down, in goal line situations, or on fourth-and-short, Gaines could easily see 35-45% of the snaps on defense as a run-down specialist. The Bills don't have a ton of those along their defensive front, and given Leonhard's stated desire to be significantly better against the run this season, it's reasonable to assume that someone like Gaines is looked at as an acquisition who can help them in achieving that goal.

August signings are often nothing more than camp bodies and tryout players, but with Greg Gaines, the Bills likely found a piece to their defense that they were missing.

title: Alabama report card: Grading the Crimson Tide after rolling through ECU
description: How did Alabama football do against East Carolina? We hand out grades for the offense, defense, coaching, special teams and overall performance.
fullText:
Alabama football wanted to make a statement in its first test of the 2026 season — and at some points, the Crimson Tide did.

The veteran defense looked ready for the rigors of SEC play. First-time starting quarterback Keelon Russell was exciting, elusive and explosive for an offense that, at its best, moved the ball consistently downfield.

But in Alabama's 48-10 win against East Carolina, the Crimson Tide showed its share of highs and lows.

Here's our postgame report card after Alabama's win against East Carolina:

ALABAMA vs EAST CAROLINA: Alabama vs East Carolina live updates: Score, highlights, analysis

KEELON RUSSELL: Live stats for Keelon Russell in first start for Alabama football vs ECU

Keelon Russell made it incredibly clear why he was picked as Alabama's starting quarterback, showing extreme elusiveness and explosiveness along with consistency moving the ball downfield. The run game is much better, too, with Daniel Hill, EJ Crowell and Russell finding daylight and falling forward and through East Carolina defenders. The Crimson Tide showed bumps along the way, whether it was Russell running for his life and taking hits or Ryan Coleman-Williams' drops and a fumble, despite an overall solid performance statistically. That was the first half. The second brought inconsistencies and an inability to move the ball until Trae'shawn Brown's 2-yard touchdown run on the first play of the fourth quarter to make the score 44-10. This is an offense that isn't a finished product and nowhere near perfect, but there was enough to show potential, potential that can be groundbreaking in the long run.

Other than one busted play that led to East Carolina's only touchdown, Alabama's defense was dominant, forcing the Pirates off the field and creating turnovers, headlined by Yhonzae Pierre's first career interception, one he returned for a score. Alabama's defense looks SEC-ready, one that continues to rotate fresh bodies in without much of a dropoff.

Saturday brought no questions about Conor Talty and Alabama's kicking game, Alex Asparuhov hit two 50-plus-yard punts and the most talked-about part of the return game was that Ryan Coleman-Williams and Dijon Lee Jr. were the ones returning.

In an offseason defined by run game improvements, from the hires of Adrian Klemm and Richard Owens to a brand new offensive line, there was significant improvement, especially when compared to a season ago against Florida State. It's emblematic of Alabama's season debut: a group of coaches prioritizing and showing what their players had worked on all offseason, a showcase of a team that developed even if it's not a finished product.

Alabama's debut was not perfect by any means, but there was enough pointing in the right direction for the Crimson Tide to leave Bryant-Denny Stadium satisfied.

Yhonzae Pierre entered 2026 with ample expectation. From taking his first career interception for a score to securing his first sack of the season, Pierre began the season exactly how he needed to — by dominating.

title: Israel says it has cleared Hezbollah fighters from tunnels under key Lebanon ridge
description: BEIRUT/JERUSALEM, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Israel's military has cleared Hezbollah fighters holed up in tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Ka...
fullText:
BEIRUT/JERUSALEM, Sept 4 (Reuters) - Israel's military has cleared Hezbollah fighters holed up in tunnels under the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Friday, though the Iran-backed group did not immediately comment.

Israel had said Hezbollah fighters were ‌embedded in tunnels under the ridge, which overlooks a wide area and had become one of the most hotly contested areas in the Israel-Hezbollah war, despite ‌a ceasefire announced in June.

"The mission was ​completed and the tunnels were cleared of terrorists," Katz said on social media, after a statement by the military late on Thursday saying it had operational control of the ridge.

The military said some Hezbollah fighters had been "eliminated", while others had fled.

A Lebanese military officer said Israeli troops had seized the southern entrances to the complex and could monitor the northern entrances through surveillance drones.

The complex included various tunnels and storage areas, some of which were not connected to one another, and it was unclear how far the troops had penetrated, and whether any fighters ‌were still there, or might have booby-trapped parts of the complex, ⁠the officer said.

Hezbollah did not immediately respond to a request for comment and Reuters was not able to verify the status of the ridge independently.

The Shi'ite Muslim group is believed to have built an underground command centre and weapons stores within the ridge and had said ⁠it would resist any Israeli assault.

ISRAEL RELEASES FIVE LEBANESE DETAINEES

Israel has expanded its military presence across swathes of southern Lebanon since launching a new campaign against Hezbollah in March.

On Friday, Israeli authorities released four people who had been held in Israeli prisons after being detained by Israeli troops in southern Lebanon. They were transferred to Lebanese authorities via the International Committee of the Red Cross, a ​day ​after one Lebanese man was released.

Israel said on Thursday that none of the five had been found ​to have ties to militant groups.

Hussein Ayyash, a 33-year-old released on Friday, said ‌he was driving in the southern Lebanese town of Kfar Tebnit nearly three months ago when Israeli soldiers approached and ordered him out of his car.

He said he was blindfolded and handcuffed, and then slept several days in various homes in southern Lebanon before being transferred into Israel and held in solitary confinement, sometimes for up to 30 days.

"Then they move you to prison, a normal room. There are places, called a cage, you sit in it. There are some people -- Syrian nationals, Lebanese nationals, Palestinian nationals -- all the nationalities, the different ones, are in prison. You get moved from room to room every once in a while, every 40 days, 30 days," Ayyash told Reuters.

He said he was asked whether ‌he had ties to Hezbollah, and was not tortured but suffered mental strain.

"You have to talk. They ​have all the information. Psychological pressure isn't easy -- you're in a country that isn't yours, you're with people ​you don't know, and you don't know when you'll leave," he said.

The Israeli ​military did not immediately respond to Reuters questions about Ayyash's detention.

Ayyash's mother, Layla Hamdan, 58, said she was delighted her son was back, ‌adding: "God willing, may all the hostages returned to their mothers and ​their families."

ISRAEL SEEKS REMAINS OF JEWISH LEADERS

The release of ​the detainees is part of confidence-building measures agreed in U.S.-brokered talks between Lebanon and Israel.

A Lebanese committee advocating for Lebanese in Israeli custody says Israel has detained dozens of people inside Lebanon over the last six months. Some have been released after days or weeks, others remain in Israeli custody.

The ICRC said on Friday ​it had not had access to anyone in Israeli detention ‌since October 2023.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said those freed this week were among a "first batch", suggesting more could be coming.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Lebanon would ​also transfer the remains of Jewish figures killed in Lebanon in the 1980s to Israel, although there were no details of names or any ​timeframe.

title: Exclusive-White House reviews candidates to replace Hegseth deputy Feinberg, sources say
description: , Erin Banco and David Jeans WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The White House has reviewed candidates to potentially replace Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg, three
fullText:
WASHINGTON/NEW YORK, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The White House has reviewed candidates to potentially replace Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg, three people familiar with the discussions told Reuters, a sign that more leadership change could come for a Pentagon already facing unusually high staff turnover.

The effort, which was ‌under way in June, has included conversations with senior lawmakers in the Senate about whether the administration's picks would have enough support to be confirmed, said two of ‌the people, one of whom added that the review was still going on as of late August. Reuters could not determine when the White House began considering candidates.

The three sources said no decision had been made to remove Feinberg from his ​post. They did not say why the White House was reviewing potential replacements and did not specify which candidates the White House was considering.

"These so-called anonymous 'sources' have no idea what they are talking about," said White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly.

"President Trump appreciates the work of Secretary Hegseth, Deputy Secretary Feinberg, and the entire Department of War, whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself," she said, referring to U.S. military operations in Iran and Venezuela.

The Pentagon denied a process was under way to replace Feinberg. Asked for comment by Reuters, Hegseth said in a ‌statement that Feinberg has his full support and "isn't going anywhere."

The Pentagon ⁠did not provide a comment from Feinberg and declined to make him available for an interview.

A departure by Feinberg, the billionaire co-founder of private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management, would be the most senior staff change for a department that has already seen a string of high-profile departures under Secretary of Defense ⁠Pete Hegseth.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned this week following months of tension with Hegseth, according to a source familiar with the matter. The Army has declined to comment on the reasons for his departure. Navy Secretary John Phelan and several senior Army leaders have also departed in recent months.

Feinberg, who vowed to accelerate U.S. munitions production, has not yet met that goal, according to analysts who say that the U.S. industrial base ​cannot ​ramp up quickly. Some defense industry executives say his task has been complicated by the slow pace of Congress ​appropriating funds despite immense pressure from the administration.

Feinberg "has worked tirelessly to rebuild our ‌Defense Industrial Base and ensure our military has everything it needs to win, and I look forward to continuing to work with him," Hegseth said in his statement to Reuters, adding, "He's doing a tremendous job for President Trump, for the Department, and for our warfighters."

Trump has increasingly expressed frustration with the lack of progress in the six-month-old Iran war, which has settled into a costly standoff between the U.S. and Iran.

One of the costs has been a drawdown of U.S. weapons stockpiles. Reuters has reported that the U.S. military faces significant shortages of certain munitions, which have alarmed Congress and military leaders.

Trump has dismissed the concerns, saying the U.S. has "far more munitions than anyone in the world."

But in an exchange with Trump at Camp David earlier this month, ‌according to the Washington Post, Hegseth blamed Feinberg for letting stockpiles of long-range guided missiles and air-defense interceptors shrink.

The ​White House has called the report "fake news." In a statement to Reuters, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said: "Secretary Hegseth did ​not mislead anyone about our munitions posture, and he did not blame Deputy Secretary Feinberg."

Appointed ​by Trump last year, Feinberg has attempted to reshape the Pentagon by ramping up the U.S. military's direct investments in companies and delivering loans to military ‌contractors through multiple offices inside the department, including the Office of Strategic ​Capital and the newly created Economic Defense Unit.

In an ​August 18 memo he sent to defense firms and seen by Reuters, Feinberg called on contractors to speed up production and provide more transparency around pricing. The Pentagon did not respond to a question about the memo.

Feinberg has also come under scrutiny on Capitol Hill, where Democratic U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren has raised concerns about whether his former firm Cerberus ​could benefit from the Pentagon's spending on its Golden Dome missile ‌defense program.

"There are no conflicts of interest between Deputy Secretary of War Steve Feinberg and Cerberus," said Parnell. "He has completely divested from Cerberus and has recused himself from ​any conversations or business relationships between the Executive Branch and Cerberus."

Cerberus did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Rabbinic group accuses Jewish entertainers of 'whitewashing antisemitism' in Mark Ruffalo defense
description: The Coalition for Jewish Values accused over 170 Jewish entertainers of whitewashing antisemitism by defending Mark Ruffalo's merger criticism.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX — A rabbinic group is calling out some Jewish entertainers for "whitewashing antisemitism" by supporting actor Mark Ruffalo after his harsh opposition to the proposed Warner Bros. Discovery-Paramount merger.

More than 170 Jewish entertainers and artists signed a letter Tuesday "proudly" voicing support for Ruffalo after he was accused of antisemitism when criticizing the proposed $111 billion merger.

Coalition for Jewish Values, which represents over 2,500 traditional, Orthodox rabbis in American public policy, said it typically does not respond when a Hollywood figure says something it finds hateful about Jews or Israel. But the group believes Ruffalo's comments forced a group of Jewish Hollywood figures that have "little knowledge of Jewish history or the nature of antisemitism" to "deny obvious bigotry."

More Than 180 Jewish Entertainers Rally Behind Actor Mark Ruffalo In Protest Letter

"Ruffalo did not merely criticize a business deal. In an August 22 Instagram post tying the Paramount-Skydance/Warner Bros. merger to Oracle's work with Israel, Ruffalo claimed that the Ellison family — who are Jewish — were 'powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world,' and framed a corporate transaction as built on 'genocide' and 'apartheid.' That is not policy criticism, but mischaracterization of civil rights for Jews and Arabs as racism, and the rescue of Jewish hostages as murder," the Coalition for Jewish Values said in a statement.

"Nonetheless, more than 170 Jewish entertainment figures rushed to sign a letter dismissing the antisemitism charge as an 'outrageous smear campaign.' To be certain, they are entitled to their ignorant and misguided views," the statement continued. "They are not, however, entitled to be taken seriously when they engage in whitewashing antisemitism, or suggest that those with sufficient discernment to recognize the oldest of anti-Jewish tropes should deny the obvious."

The group said that "America set itself apart from much of the world precisely by declaring hatred of Jews unwelcome, regardless of who dressed it up as righteousness," and feels "Ruffalo would do well to remember that he owes much of his career to the Founding Fathers who made America so hospitable, and the Jews who fled persecution in Europe to build new homes for their children in a friendlier land."

John Cusack Stands In 'Solidarity' With Mark Ruffalo Amid Paramount's Antisemitism Allegation

"It is some of those children, working in New York in the early 20th century, who created Marvel Comics and invented The Incredible Hulk," the group said.

Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, told Fox News Digital that Ruffalo's remarks were "embarrassing" and that Ruffalo presented a "mythical inversion" of the situation in the Middle East.

Ruffalo was accused of invoking "antisemitic tropes" by Paramount after the Marvel star shared a video from August of Safra Catz, an Oracle executive vice chair and Paramount board member, discussing technology Oracle used to assist Israel after the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attack.

He linked Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, to financing behind the proposed acquisition and suggested the merger would be used to push "oppression."

"These 'really profoundly scary technologies' will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you," Ruffalo said. "Look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle."

Antisemitic Violence Reaches Deadliest Level Since 1994, New Global Report Finds

Among the Jewish artists who signed the letter were Abbi Jacobson, Alex Winter, Gina Gershon, Ilana Glazer, James Schamus, Joel Coen, Larry Charles, Kate Berlant, Naomi Klein, Sarah Sherman, Jane Schoenbrun, Todd Haynes and Tony Kushner, denied Ruffalo's comments were antisemitic, arguing that the executives Ruffalo criticized had "themselves have explicitly linked to their support for the ongoing depredations being visited on the people of Palestine and their silencing of critics of those horrors."

The celebrities also argued that a majority of American Jews now believe that Israel committed war crimes against Gaza, with a significant portion believing Israel is guilty of genocide. They called for an end to "spurious charges of antisemitism" against people like Ruffalo.

Ruffalo previously denied pushing antisemitism in a statement to Fox News Digital after Paramount's original condemnation.

"The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest," Ruffalo said. "Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people."

title: With a wary eye on Russia, Finland runs Europe's largest civil defense exercise since WWII
description: In a civil defense shelter hewn into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation le...
fullText:
KUOPIO, Finland (AP) — In a civil defense shelter hewn into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation levels as they take part in an exercise to turn a cave into a place of safety for thousands of people.

Inside, in what is normally a sports hall, hundreds of people are sleeping overnight on trestle beds.

More than 2,000 people including volunteers and students are taking part in the biggest civil defense exercise in Europe since the end of World War II. In the scenario, critical infrastructure in the central Finnish city of Kuopio, including power and water, has been disrupted by cyberattacks and there's the threat of missile strikes from Finland's neighbor, Russia.

The goal is for local authorities and ordinary people to rehearse what they would do if they came under attack for real.

But while underground bunkers and shelters may offer some protection from missiles, they are no defense against the campaign of sabotage and disruption that Western officials say Russia is carrying out across Europe. That has involved setting fires, attacking water facilities and power stations, and sending drones for sabotage into European Union airspace.

Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 830 miles (1,300 kilometers) from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle. In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Until then, Finns were prepared to defend themselves against Russia largely alone.

Finland's defense, said retired Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, relies not only on the military but on the "mindset" of ordinary Finns who are ready to take responsibility for their country's security.

Muhonen, who organized the exercise in Kuopio, said that comes partly from the system of conscription which continued in Finland, even after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Not everyone is happy about doing national service but "it's our duty to serve and protect this country like people have before us. That's why we have our independence," said Jyry Pietikainen, 23, a conscript who was taught how to run the Kuopio shelter overnight.

Finland also needs to learn lessons from Ukraine, Muhonen said.

While the biggest shelter in Kuopio can fit 7,000 people, Ukrainians sometimes only have a few minutes to run to a subway station or underground parking lot. That means people need a shelter they can reach easily that offers some form of protection — not necessarily one that can withstand a nuclear attack, he said.

Dmytro Untila, 20, a Ukrainian student at the university in Kuopio, was at home in Odesa when Russian missiles struck his city on Feb. 24, 2022, the first day of the war. He sheltered in the entrance hall of his building because he didn't have anywhere else to go, he said.

Training for such a situation would have definitely helped in Ukraine, he said, "because nobody knew this could happen."

The biggest threat to energy infrastructure in the Kuopio region is heavy snowfall, storms and bad weather, said Juha Räsänen, CEO at the Savon Voima electricity company.

But since the invasion of Ukraine, and the company's decision to stop buying Russian biofuel, the number of cyberattacks against the network has significantly increased, Räsänen said.

Last year, engineers also found at least 10 stickers placed on particularly vulnerable parts of the energy network infrastructure. Other energy companies in Finland have also found them and don't know where they came from, he said.

"If there was an explosion at that point, it could destroy a whole dam," Räsänen said. Drones have also been spotted over power lines but those responsible have not been identified, he said.

It is not possible to guard against all threats, Räsänen said, which is why it's important people are prepared to look after themselves without help for at least 72 hours — if the power supply goes out, or if water becomes undrinkable.

The Finnish Security and Intelligence Service said it investigated "a wide range of observations" and found nothing of concern.

Since 2022, people have been more vigilant because of the security situation and therefore have reported things like reflective stickers related to land survey works, it said in a statement. Drone sightings, it said, have "largely been explained by everyday occurrences."

"Small things are happening all the time," including Russian jamming of GPS signals, said Vuokko Lahtinen, 32, who was visiting a sauna in Kuopio.

For that reason, "the best defense of Finland is to make it not worth attacking," she said.

That relies on the country's military and defense forces but also Finnish people who feel like "we have something we want to fight for," she said.

In Finland, she said, there is a "general feeling of responsibility," which has grown out of local community groups and even initiatives such as recycling.

"On a very simple daily level, if you do things that matter, then it has a butterfly-wing effect," Lahtinen said.

In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11% of its territory, and more than 400,000 people, around 12% of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.

At Kuopio's veterans' museum, Risto Mönkkönen, 95, showed AP a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.

"I cannot forget it," he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father's friends.

Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.

Aili Toivanen, 92, told AP she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.

The first time, she looked back and saw her home burning — set on fire by Finnish soldiers who did not want to leave anything behind, she said. The second time, she said, the Soviet air force bombed the family's departing train and they jumped out, hiding in ditches before they took refuge in Kuopio.

When Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, she said, with tears in her eyes, that she worried she would have to leave her home for a third time.

At the shelter in Kuopio, thousands of people filed in, including schoolchildren and university students.

"Kids would need to know this, because they might have to do something alone. The adults can't always help," said Amanda Hill, 11, whose school studied in the shelter for the day.

Sitting on the floor of the shelter with his fellow conscripts, Pietikainen explained why it's not crazy to practice what happens in a crisis.

"We're Finns, so we're kind of pessimistic about life in a way," but history shows what can happen with Russia, he said.

When it comes to the threats from Moscow, Muhonen said, "don't believe what they say but observe what they do."

title: GoPro Says It's Moving into Data Centers as Part of a $285M Merger
description: The company says its also planning a push into defense, robotics and aerospace.
fullText:
It's also planning a push into defense, robotics and aerospace.

GoPro is the latest surprising name to move into the AI data center market amid a merger with an optical-photonics company called Starman Optical. The shareholders of GoPro, which will remain publicly listed, will receive $285 million when the deal closes and retain around 10 percent ownership. GoPro's outstanding debt of around $92 million will be paid too.

GoPro is following in the footsteps of shoemaker Allbirds by making an unexpected shift into AI infrastructure. title: Israel captures top Hamas commander in Gaza strike, defense minister says

The Israel Defense Forces captured Hamas' head of general security during a raid in Gaza, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said.

An Israeli security official identified the Hamas leader as Mu'in al-Arabid, head of the General Security Apparatus, saying he was arrested during an Israeli incursion deep inside Hamas territory in Gaza. Hamas Struggles To Fill Leadership Ranks As Israel Hunts Oct 7 Terrorists

Even after that, the IDF will remain in Gaza along defensive lines and ensure the security of the western Negev communities. Any attempt to bypass the security zone through aerial launches will be met with a harsh response," he added.

Kushner Touts Unprecedented Iran Contacts As Tehran Denies Trump Backchannel

"It's going to have to be based on actions and steps, and I hope it will be true."

title: What We Learned About College Football in Week 0

fullText:
North Carolina is better – but probably not very good

Hats off to Bill Belichick and the Tar Heels for topping TCU 15-10 in week 0, after being completely dismantled by the Horned Frogs to kick off the 2025 season. The defense has shown signs of improvement, especially along the defensive line. However, TCU's offense seems to be a bit of a mess, and were held scoreless after scoring 10 points in their first two possessions. UNC also has some work cut out for them on offense and needs to find ways to generate more explosive plays. It was a nice start, but not sure UNC will go very far in year two of the Belichick experiment.

USC and Florida State had similar outcomes, but very different games

USC took down San Jose State, 42-26, while Florida State earned a week one victory over New Mexico State, 34-17. Neither outcome looks all that impressive, but the final scores are a bit deceiving. The Trojans built an early lead, then took their foot off the gas in the second half. The starters were out of the game by the fourth quarter, helping San Jose State come away with a 23-7 output in the final stanza. Meanwhile, Florida State could not pull away from New Mexico State and were forced to play four quarters. USC sure looked like they are a playoff contender, while Florida State may finish with yet another losing season – and be searching for a new head coach at some point this fall.

Virginia may be sticking around for a while

Virginia just missed out on the playoffs last season after losing to Duke in the ACC Championship Game. It was a nice story, but many dismissed the Cavaliers as a one-year wonder. In fact, they only appeared on one ballot in the preseason AP poll. However, it sure looks like they will have a number next to their name soon, and could be in the thick of the race for the ACC crown again. The offense looked sharp and the defense completely dominated NC State in what was expected to be a competitive contest. In case you were wondering, Beau Pribula had an enticing stat line while leading the team in passing and rushing – 9 of 11 for for two touchdowns and no interceptions, with another 110 yards on the ground on 15 carries.

Memphis has an early lead on the playoff race

Both UNLV and Memphis had their sights set on the playoffs this year – and the Tigers got a huge boost with their 27-21 victory over the Rebels. This will set up a huge showdown on Sept. 12 when Memphis visits Boise State. Charles Huff has been working his way up the coaching ranks, and may be a P4 head coach in 2027.

title: Accused NC killer mom plans insanity defense — as retired judge says more may follow Lindsay Clancy strategy
description: Andrea Faust's insanity defense in her son's killing draws direct parallels to Lindsay Clancy's postpartum psychosis case as jurors deliberate.
fullText:
The insanity defense planned by a North Carolina mother accused of killing her son has drawn parallels to Lindsay Clancy's trial and raised questions about whether it could become prevalent in criminal cases.

Andrea Faust, 41, is charged with murder and attempted murder in the Feb. 12 death of her 3-year-old son and the attempted murder of her 2-year-old son at their home in Durham, North Carolina.

Her attorneys have filed notice that they intend to rely on defenses of not guilty by reason of insanity and diminished capacity, WRAL reported.

The case is drawing parallels to Clancy's Massachusetts trial. Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu said he expects similar defenses to be raised more often as the Clancy case draws national attention to postpartum mental-health conditions.

Lindsay Clancy Didn't Show 'Break With Reality' As Jury Weighs Psychosis Defense: Susan Smith Prosecutor

Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility in the 2023 deaths of her three children. Her defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argue she understood her actions and acted deliberately.

Jurors ended a second day of deliberations Friday without reaching a verdict. They will return on Monday morning to continue working toward a verdict.

In Faust's case, the filing does not establish that she was legally insane or had diminished capacity. Her attorney, Nicole Galinsky, told the local outlet that a defense expert concluded Faust could not distinguish right from wrong during the alleged murders.

"Andrea and Lindsay's cases are eerily similar, though not entirely the same," Galinsky told Fox News Digital.

Galinsky noted that Faust was not suffering from postpartum psychosis.

"However, both women were known to be loving, doting, responsible mothers who were worried about and caring for their children up until the very second they decided to kill them," Galinsky said, adding that Faust and Clancy were both struggling with similar issues, including hallucinations, hospitalizations and mental health.

"Neither woman did this out of the blue," Galinsky said in an email. "Both were struggling enormously with their mental health. But, like most women and almost all moms, they were just trying to get through each day, care for their children, be a good mom/wife/employee. Both were seeking help from doctors who weren't really taking their concerns seriously.

"Both of these cases highlight the failure in our society to take women and mothers seriously when it comes to their mental health. Both of these women advocated for themselves countless times and—for what? It got them nowhere.

"I am hopeful that our case will demonstrate how to properly treat and rehabilitate a woman living her own worst nightmare. Lindsay Clancy was not given that luxury."

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

Lu said society and the legal system have not fully understood the effects postpartum mental illness can have on behavior and criminal responsibility.

"Most of the time, these criminal responsibility, insanity, mental health defenses are unsuccessful," Lu told Fox News Digital.

Lindsay Clancy's Family Was 'Very Concerned' About Her Mental Health In The Months Before She Killed Her Kids

Although he is not a mental-health expert, Lu said the Clancy trial has challenged and changed his own understanding of what a person might experience.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

"I had no real understanding of what a person like Ms. Clancy was going through until this trial," he said.

Faust was found incapable of proceeding to trial in March after court records documented serious concerns about her mental health and safety, according to WRAL.

Central Regional Hospital later found her capable of proceeding as of May 21. Her attorney said another evaluation would examine her mental state at the time of the alleged offenses.

Lu said mental-health defenses should receive more serious consideration because they can explain behavior and reduce moral culpability. But allegations involving children create an especially difficult path with jurors, he said.

"These cases should have legs," Lu said, "but unfortunately society and juries don't give them much credence."

title: Billions in US aid to Ukraine under microscope as corruption rocks Zelenskyy’s inner circle
description: Over 24 federal agencies oversee billions in U.S. defense aid to Ukraine as Zelenskyy dismisses officials amid widening anti-corruption probes, expert says.
fullText:
Washington is relying on extensive safeguards and dozens of oversight agencies to scrutinize and protect billions of dollars in U.S. aid to Ukraine amid the country's continuing struggle with corruption, a regional security expert said Sunday.

The oversight comes as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's inner circle faces renewed political pressure from widening investigations, with several senior officials and aides resigning, being dismissed or facing investigations since 2025.

Zelenskyy dismissed Iryna Mudra, a deputy head of the presidential office, on Aug. 19 as anti-corruption investigators pursued a money-laundering case involving another deputy head of the office.

Investigators have not named Mudra as a suspect, The Associated Press reported.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

"Of course, in all of the former Soviet Union countries, there is significant corruption," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.

"A lot more work needs to be done. But we know, at least on the U.S. side, as we're providing support for their military, we have a lot of mechanisms," she said before explaining how dozens of agencies are working on oversight of U.S. aid to Ukraine.

The U.S. committed $67.8 billion in defense articles and services to Ukraine from February 2022 through March 2026 through the Presidential Drawdown Authority, the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative and Foreign Military Financing, congressional reports show.

That support is part of a broader U.S. response to the war.

About $195 billion has been appropriated for Operation Atlantic Resolve, including funds to replenish U.S. weapons stocks, support U.S. military operations in Europe and provide economic, development and humanitarian assistance, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

As Trump's Nato Gamble Pays Off, Envoy Names Allies He's Still Watching

"Over 24 federal agencies are involved in oversight," Filipetti said. "To make certain that there are no consequences to the U.S. taxpayer, to our equipment in terms of the corruption issue, U.S. contributions are very much protected."

In recent months, however, senior Ukrainian officials have resigned, been dismissed or faced scrutiny by the country's independent anti-corruption bodies, including Nabu.

Those developments include Andriy Yermak's Nov. 28, 2025, resignation after investigators searched his premises and Mudra's Aug. 19 dismissal during a money-laundering probe.

Former Deputy Prime Minister Olha Stefanishyna was dismissed by Zelenskyy as Ukraine's ambassador to the U.S. on Aug. 3, two days before a suspicion notice was served against her, according to the Kyiv Post.

He also fired Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov on July 15 in a broader reshuffle over internal wartime disagreements which sparked protests across the nation.

Zelenskyy Pressures Us And Europe For More 'Air Defense' Assistance Amid Ongoing War With Russia

In interviews after he left government, Fedorov also complained about what he described as ingrained corruption and patronage networks, Reuters reported.

"We've seen that Zelenskyy is taking really seriously the criticisms of corruption, and every time there is an allegation, he moves very swiftly to remove those individuals from the government," Filipetti said.

"And the fact that there are these independent bodies is, I think, really important. They're listening to them. They're making sure that they're trying to root it out as much as humanly possible."

title: Mike Elko eyes 'winning plays' for Texas A&M in 2026

fullText:
Playing "winning football" sounds vague on the surface, and heading into Mike Elko's third season at the helm, it's clear that the program is in the right direction, but back-to-back losses to Texas and Miami in the first round of the College Football Playoff were the antithesis of what we saw throughout the 2025 season.

Under first-year offensive coordinator Holmon Wiggins, the expectation is that Marcel Reed will return to utilizing his dual-threat skill set more often, getting outside the pocket, especially on play action where he has thrived since becoming the full-time starter. During Thursday's press conference, Mike Elko said taking another step toward making "winning plays" in key moments has been a clear focus, starting with finishing strong every practice, while his team's mental makeup will be tested throughout the nine-game SEC schedule.

"We got to continue to be the team that steps up and makes those winning plays in those moments, and that's what we did in those games… That's what we didn't do in the playoff game."

"The more parity sets in, which it clearly is, and the more that the top comes down a little bit and the bottom comes up… It's going to come down to winning plays."

Situations where Marcel Reed is dropping back in 12 personnel and needing to make perfect throws in tight windows must be avoided, if possible, to avoid placing added pressure; this starts with a strong run game, which will open up play-action looks and allow the Aggies' wide receivers to make plays after the catch.

title: A Ukrainian air-defense sergeant says missiles aren't his most challenging shortage. It's the gear that finds enemy targets.
description: Ukraine uses MANPADS to down Russian drones, jets, and aircraft, but to be effective, teams need batteries and ways to find targets.
fullText:
A Ukrainian sergeant said supporting gear is harder to get for his air defense unit than missiles.

It uses MANPADS that down Russian jets and aircraft, but needs batteries and ways to find targets.

Equipment like drone detectors and electronic warfare systems is "hard to get," he said.

The hardest shortage facing one Ukrainian shoulder-fired air-defense unit isn't necessarily missiles, its battery sergeant told Business Insider. It's some of the equipment that helps crews find targets and keep their systems running.

The soldier, who uses the call sign Yankee, serves in a front-line unit equipped with man-portable air-defense systems, or MANPADS, which fire shoulder-launched missiles able to engage low-flying aircraft, as well as cruise missiles and drones.

Weapons like these, which include the US Stinger, Polish Piorun, and Soviet-designed Igla, have been a key part of Ukraine's short-range air defense in front-line areas, protecting troops and operations from attacks.

Yankee said that for him, at least, one of the hardest things "is finding resources. Secondary resources, not the weaponry, but electronic warfare stuff."

He said some of the devices that help his team detect threats and keep its equipment working are "hard to get." What is hardest to find is "mostly electronics."

"I'm talking more about devices that locate the drones and warn you," Yankee said. "I'm talking about stuff like EcoFlows, batteries, big batteries, because we have a shortage of them, just in general, just a mass shortage."

Ukrainian soldiers are increasingly using drone detectors, including small handheld or vehicle-mounted models, to warn of certain incoming enemy drones by detecting their radio frequencies.

EcoFlows are portable power stations that can power or recharge essential gear such as radios and communications equipment, Starlink terminals, laptops and tablets, drone equipment, electronic warfare systems, and sensors.

These, and batteries in general, are especially important because soldiers are often far from power outlets, and Russian attacks often shut down energy infrastructure. Running a portable generator would be much louder and might reveal their positions.

Electronic warfare systems are also vital for Ukraine as it tries to disrupt Russia's communications and jam its drones.

Despite their importance, this equipment isn't always easy for units to obtain in sufficient quantities. Some of the gear is much newer and less readily available than supplies like ammunition. And while demand is high, some equipment still isn't being produced in large quantities. In some cases, there are also distribution bottlenecks that affect availability.

Unlike many Western militaries, Ukraine's military doesn't have a highly centralized system for weapons procurement. Units often buy or receive gear themselves, including through crowdfunding.

There are advantages to this setup for rapid innovation because units engage manufacturers directly, but the system can also result in uneven distribution, leaving some units facing shortages.

Ukrainian foundations, units, and other groups that are involved in sourcing and crowdfunding equipment for troops often ask for gear like batteries and detectors, with some describing them as items that air defenders regularly need.

MANPADS and the units that operate them are important for Ukraine. Units, service members, and officials have reported missiles taking down Russian drones, helicopters, and aircraft, and Western analysts have credited MANPADS with making penetrating low-altitude Russian fixed-wing and helicopter sorties too costly for Russia to continue.

A report last year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, said that Ukraine's integration of MANPADS operators into its air defense teams forced Russian pilots to choose between flying high and being targeted by ground-based air defenses or flying low and facing MANPAD missiles. These short-range defenses relieved the pressure on Ukraine's ground-based systems, allowing them to "survive and eventually recover."

Yankee's unit provides air defense for infantry who need to get to the zero line, the far edge of the front line, and, as a result, "we participate in battle," he said.

He said that conditions there can be so dangerous that moving just 300 meters can take 7 days of waiting for safe conditions and protection. Moving even that short distance, he said, "can be like a question of life and death."

Yankee spoke with Business Insider at Operation Legio, a Norway-led multinational program that trains and equips Ukrainian forces, including at a purpose-built camp in Poland. He said he was learning NATO standards and tactics, combining Western practices with his existing battle-won skills before returning to Ukraine.

Yankee said he uses the Stinger and Igla systems. Ukrainian soldiers have, at times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, reported shortages of MANPADS missiles, saying those shortages allowed Russian forces to be bolder because they knew the Ukrainians couldn't try to stop as many of their attacks.

But Ukraine's military has not suffered critical shortages of them the way it has with larger, surface-to-air missiles, and allies have announced new deliveries throughout the war.

Not everything is consistent across the force though. Ukraine's military disseminates weapons and ammunition according to operational need, so one unit could be well supplied for critical missions while another comes up short.

Asked about the standoff, he told reporters it was "frustrating, but I'm focused on the season."

His trainer posted, then deleted, a message on Thursday saying New England should trade him. That remains the loudest anyone in Gonzalez's circle has been all summer.

title: Opinion - Trump picked a trade fight with Canada. US defense firms may pay the price
description: None of what Washington wanted on defense was ever going to be delivered by threat.
fullText:
Washington went into last week's trade talks with Canada looking for more than relief on dairy and alcohol. The administration wanted Ottawa to complete its F-35 purchase, buy American radar planes as part of joining President Trump's Golden Dome missile defense project and grant the U.S. a right of first refusal on Canadian critical minerals.

None of what Washington wanted on defense was ever going to be delivered by threat. A tariff can be imposed and enforced at the border. Completing the F-35 order, joining Golden Dome, opening Canadian mineral reserves to American companies are different. No Canadian government can be forced into them, because each one requires Ottawa to keep saying yes, year after year, as contracts get signed and budgets get voted. Squeezing Canada on trade doesn't make that yes more likely. It makes those choices harder to defend in Ottawa.

The administration has spent years telling allies to spend more on defense. Canada is finally doing it: Carney says his government will put half a trillion dollars into defense investment over the next decade. Until now, roughly 70 percent of Canada's defense spending has gone to U.S. suppliers. Carney's new defense industrial strategy wants Canadian firms to capture that same share instead. The trade fight didn't start that pivot, but it has strengthened the case for it.

The F-35 is the clearest case. Canada contracted for 88 aircraft, but Carney ordered the purchase reviewed after Trump's first tariff offensive last year. Washington wanted reassurance in these talks that Canada would finish the buy. It left without it.

The minerals dispute cuts the same way. The Pentagon has good reason to want secure North American supplies instead of Chinese ones. But demanding privileged access while punishing Canadian industries with tariffs was never going to produce a deal. Carney has already rejected exclusive access and called deeper minerals cooperation one of the casualties of the failed talks.

Since 1956, the U.S.-Canada Defense Production Sharing Agreement has tied the two countries' defense industries together closely enough that more than 110 Canadian companies have taken part in the F-35 supply chain. Washington built that arrangement, and benefited from it, because Canadian procurement usually reinforced an American-centered continental defense economy. That was the quiet assumption behind seven decades of cooperation: it didn't need to be re-earned in every budget cycle.

The defense relationship was already showing strain before the latest talks collapsed. In May, the Pentagon suspended the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, which had coordinated U.S.-Canada military consultation since 1940, citing Canada's slow progress on defense spending and its stalled F-35 decision. That happened three months before last week's collapse.

Golden Dome exposes the same problem from the other direction. Canada is already investing in NORAD modernization with new radar and surveillance for the northern approaches that any continental missile defense system would need. Canadian participation still requires Canadian consent and Canadian money. Tariff pressure doesn't make that participation more likely. It makes routine cooperation look like something Ottawa has to keep defending politically.

No serious Canadian government is going to withdraw from NORAD. Geography leaves both countries with too much at stake. The real damage will show up in the next round of choices: aircraft, sensors, industrial partnerships, as Canada decides where a much larger defense budget actually goes.

Trump wanted Canada to shoulder more of its own defense burden. He may get exactly that. What his administration hasn't reckoned with is how much of that new Canadian money will still flow south, after a year of tactics that turned dependence on the United States into a political liability in Ottawa.

Andrew Latham is a professor of international relations at Macalester College in Saint Paul, Minn., a senior fellow at the Institute for Peace and Diplomacy.

fullText:
Anthropic ​argued designation as ‘supply-chain risk’ could cost billions ‌in lost business ‌and reputational harm

A US judge ruled on Thursday that the Trump administration broke the law when it designated Anthropic as a supply chain risk earlier this year, finding that the government had unlawfully targeted the AI firm for refusing to comply with defense department demands.

“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Judge Rita Lin said in a 59-page decision.

Lin’s ruling barred the federal agencies named in the lawsuit from enforcing Donald Trump’s order to stop using Anthropic’s tools and overturned the designation of the company as a “supply chain risk” by the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. The status, usually reserved for foreign firms, would have blocked government agencies from doing business with Anthropic.

The case emerged out of a months-long feud between Anthropic and the Pentagon at the start of the year. Anthropic refused to allow the government to use its Claude AI model for fully autonomous lethal weapons or domestic mass surveillance, resulting in Hegseth accusing the company of “arrogance and betrayal”.

Lin put a temporary pause on the government’s punitive measures in March, stating that the government’s actions looked like an attempt to “cripple Anthropic” for exercising its first amendment rights. The ruling this week makes that temporary suspension permanent, although the government may appeal.

“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said.

Lin’s ruling is a victory for Anthropic, which had warned that the supply chain risk designation could cost the company billions of dollars and complicate its business model. Anthropic is also planning an IPO later this year that could value the firm at $2tn and raise $100bn, exceeding the record set by SpaceX in June.

Anthropic still faces legal hurdles related to the supply chain risk designation, however, as the outcome of a second lawsuit in Washington DC is still pending. That case will be heard by a three-judge panel, two of whom are Trump appointees who have expressed skepticism about Anthropic’s arguments.

Anthropic says that AI models are not reliable enough to be safely used in autonomous weapons ‌and that it opposes domestic surveillance as a violation of rights, but the Pentagon says private companies should not be able to constrain military action.

In its 9 March lawsuit, Anthropic alleged the government violated its right to free speech under the first amendment of the constitution by retaliating against its views on AI safety. The company said it was not given a chance to dispute the designation, in violation of its fifth amendment right to due process.

“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice,” Lin said, “the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless.”

Anthropic’s designation was the first time a US company had been publicly categorized as a supply-chain risk under an obscure government-procurement statute aimed at protecting military systems ​from foreign sabotage.
